title: Maximum Likelihood, Fall 2026
text:
This is the course website for PLSC 606J, Maximum Likelihood Estimation, Fall 2026. The course is an advanced course in data science focusing on maximum likelihood methods and their applications in political science.

title: Slides
text:
Lecture slides and notes will be linked here as the semester proceeds.

Linear Model Prediction Methods — prediction and quantities of interest in the linear model (at-means and average effects; ML, delta, and simulation-based uncertainty), previewing the methods we generalize to nonlinear models.
Binary Response Models — building a maximum-likelihood model for a binary outcome: why the linear probability model fails, the latent-variable and random-utility motivations, the likelihood and link functions, and interpretation via predicted probabilities, marginal effects, and odds.
Likelihood Theory & Estimation Mechanics — what a likelihood is and how it differs from a probability; the estimation machine and how little of it changes from one model to the next; analytic methods and closed-form solutions, and where they fail; and the two derivatives — the score and the Hessian — that locate the estimate and set its standard error.
Maximizing the Log-Likelihood Function — Newton–Raphson from the ground up: where the method comes from, what its two halves do, one step worked by hand, then the whole loop run to convergence on a real logit, with an animated climb, the iteration log, starting values, and the properties that justify the estimator.
Prediction Methods for MLE Models — quantities of interest from nonlinear models: at-means and average effects, building a scenario’s linear prediction, King–Tomz–Wittenberg simulation, ML and delta-method standard errors with end-point transformation, the bootstrap, average effects bounded two ways, and guidance on which approach and which technique to choose.

title: Binary Response Models
text:
How can we model a binary \(y\) variable?
Does OLS (the linear probability model) work sufficiently well?
How can we build a maximum likelihood model that does work?




Before we get into the details, here is where we are going. Every limited-\(y\) model in this course — binary, count, ordered, duration — is built the same way, following the same short recipe:






Building a maximum likelihood model




Observe \(y\); consider its distribution; write down its PDF (or PMF).1
Write the joint probability of the data under that distribution.
Rewrite the joint probability as a likelihood.
Simplify — take logs.
Parameterize — make the distribution’s parameter a function of covariates, \(x\beta\) (the systematic component).
Choose a link function \(F\) that connects \(x\beta\) to that parameter and respects its bounds.



That is the whole process - we’ll follow this for much of the semester. The rest of these notes walk through these steps for the binary case: I motivate why we leave OLS behind, build the likelihood step by step, estimate it, and then evaluate the estimates.

title: Binary Response Models
text:
Example — Democratic Peace data
As a running example we’ll consider the Democratic Peace data from Oneal and Russett (1997) (ISQ). The unit is the dyad-year, \(y\) is the presence of a militarized dispute, and key covariates include shared border, the lower of the two dyad Polity scores, the capabilities ratio, and an alliance indicator. The substantive expectation: as the minimum democracy score in the dyad rises, the probability of a MID should fall.

Predictions out of bounds


code
# I fit the two binary models and OLS on the same specification, to compare
# what each one predicts.
m_logit <- glm(dispute ~ border + deml + lncaprat + ally,
               family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = dp)
m_probit <- glm(dispute ~ border + deml + lncaprat + ally,
                family = binomial(link = "probit"), data = dp)
m_ols   <- lm(dispute ~ border + deml + lncaprat + ally, data = dp)

preds <- tibble(
  logit   = predict(m_logit, type = "response"),
  ols     = predict(m_ols),
  dispute = factor(dp$dispute)
)

n_oob <- sum(preds$ols < 0)   # OLS predictions below the probability floor

ggplot(preds, aes(x = logit, y = ols, color = dispute)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.11, y = -0.11,
           label = paste(format(n_oob, big.mark = ","), "OLS predictions below 0"),
           color = "red", size = 3.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = bu_two) +
  labs(title = "Predictions from logit and OLS",
       x = "logit prediction (probability)",
       y = "OLS prediction") +
  theme_minimal()








Figure 1





About 12% of the OLS predictions fall below zero. None exceed one here, but only because disputes are rare and the fitted values stay low; with a more common outcome we’d see predictions above one as well. Either way, a number outside \([0,1]\) is not a probability, whatever else it is.


Heteroskedastic, non-normal residuals


code
tibble(resid = residuals(m_ols), dispute = factor(dp$dispute)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = resid, color = dispute)) +
  geom_density() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_color_manual(values = bu_two) +
  labs(title = "Density of OLS residuals", x = "residual", y = "density") +
  theme_minimal()









The residuals bunch around the values that produce \(\{0,1\}\) outcomes from a linear fit. In fact the distribution looks more binomial than normal — clustered near zero and one — which shouldn’t surprise us, since \(y\) only ever takes the values zero and one and the residuals are just \(u = y - \widehat{y}\). So they aren’t going to be normal, and they aren’t going to be homoskedastic.

title: Binary Response Models
section: So when is the LPM appropriate?
text:
So when is the LPM appropriate?
The best answer is never.

There seems to be a mild trend in the discipline to rehabilitate the LPM, though it’s not clear why — it’s hard to find statements about the advantages of doing so in any particular setting, or about the disadvantages of estimating a logit or probit that would lead us to prefer the LPM.

OLS is a rockin’ estimator, but it’s just not well suited to limited \(y\) variables. Efforts to rehabilitate the LPM are like putting lipstick on a pig.

title: Binary Response Models
text:
Examples of limited dependent variables
Binary \(y\) is just one kind of limited variable. The same logic — build the model around the distribution of what we actually observe — carries through the whole course. A few of the types we’ll meet:

binary variables: 0 = peace, 1 = war; 0 = didn’t vote, 1 = voted.
unordered (nominal) categories: which car you buy — Honda, Toyota, Ford, Buick; vote choice across several candidates; policy options.
ordered variables with few values: many survey responses (disagree / neutral / agree).
counts: the number of militarized disputes a dyad has in a year; episodes of torture in a country-year; arrests; doctor visits — \(0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)
time to an event: how long a civil war lasts; how long a leader survives in office; time until a patient relapses.

Each gets its own distribution and its own link, but the recipe is always the same — which is the whole point of building these models from the distribution up.

title: Binary Response Models
text:
The latent variable motivation
Imagine a latent continuous variable \(y^*\) that lives on the real line:
\[
y_i^* = x_i\beta + \varepsilon_i
\]
We don’t observe \(y^*\) directly (if we did, we’d probably be using OLS). We observe a thresholded version of it:
\[
y_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } y_i^* > 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } y_i^* \leq 0 \end{cases}
\]
The probability of observing \(y_i = 1\) is the probability that \(y_i^*\) exceeds the threshold:
\[
\begin{aligned}
Pr(y_i = 1 \mid x_i)
   &= Pr(y_i^* > 0)                  && \text{(threshold)} \\
   &= Pr(x_i\beta+\varepsilon_i > 0)                  && \text{(threshold restated)} \\
   &= Pr(\varepsilon_i > -x_i\beta)  && \text{(isolate the error)} \\
   &= 1 - F_\varepsilon(-x_i\beta)   && \text{(right tail)} \\
   &= F_\varepsilon(x_i\beta)        && \text{(symmetry)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Take the equalities in turn:

(threshold) — the step to \(Pr(y_i^* > 0)\) is the measurement step: we record a one exactly when the latent \(y_i^*\) clears the threshold, so \(Pr(y_i=1)\) just is \(Pr(y_i^* > 0)\).
(isolate the error) — the step to \(Pr(\varepsilon_i > -x_i\beta)\) substitutes \(y_i^* = x_i\beta + \varepsilon_i\) and isolates the only random piece, \(\varepsilon_i\): given \(x_i\), the systematic part \(x_i\beta\) is fixed, so a “one” requires the unobserved \(\varepsilon_i\) to exceed \(-x_i\beta\); the observed factors set a bar, and the error has to clear it. This is the substantive line, and the same object a random-utility model produces (see the note below).
(right tail) — the step to \(1 - F_\varepsilon(-x_i\beta)\) is where the CDF enters, and with it something we can actually compute. A greater-than probability on \(\varepsilon_i\) is an upper tail, and an upper tail is one minus the CDF: \(Pr(\varepsilon_i > c) = 1 - F_\varepsilon(c)\), here with \(c = -x_i\beta\). Up to now we had an event — the error clearing the bar; this rewrites it as a function of \(x_i\beta\), namely \(F_\varepsilon\) itself. That function is the link, and it is what we parameterize and drop into the likelihood to estimate. No \(F\), no estimator.
(symmetry) — the step to \(F_\varepsilon(x_i\beta)\) uses the symmetry of \(F_\varepsilon\) about zero such that \(1 - F_\varepsilon(-a) = F_\varepsilon(a)\). What it buys is the tidy, estimable form \(Pr(y_i=1) = F_\varepsilon(x_i\beta)\): the CDF read at the linear predictor directly, increasing in \(x_i\beta\) (more of the linear prediction \(x_i\beta\), more probability) and evaluated at the same \(x_i\beta\) OLS would use. That is the form we parameterize and fit. Both the normal and the logistic are symmetric, so both collapse to it; an asymmetric error (the Gumbel, hence complementary log-log) does not, and keeps the \(1 - F_\varepsilon(-x_i\beta)\) shape.







The random-utility motivation



The latent variable has a behavioral interpretation you have already encountered in formal theory. Let \(y_i^*\) be the net utility of one alternative over the other — the utility of option 1 minus the utility of option 0. The labels 0 and 1 are arbitrary: the two options could be two candidates, two commuting modes, two ice cream flavors. Split it the same way: \(x_i\beta\) is the systematic (representative) utility difference — the part explained by observed characteristics — and \(\varepsilon_i\) is the idiosyncratic part, the unobserved, agent-specific taste shock. An agent picks option 1 when its net utility is positive, \(y_i^* > 0\), which is exactly \(\varepsilon_i > -x_i\beta\): the individual taste shock has to be large enough to overcome whatever the observed factors imply. So the middle term of the derivation is a choice rule, and the binary model falls straight out of the utility theory — a direct line from the behavioral model to the estimator, rather than a latent variable posited from nowhere.
Two things follow. First, the distribution we assume for \(\varepsilon_i\) is a model of the unobserved utility: assume those shocks are logistic and we get the logit; assume normal, we get the probit. Choosing the link is choosing how unmodeled tastes are distributed. Second, nothing here needs there to be only two options. Give each alternative \(j\) its own utility \(U_{ij} = x_i\beta_j + \varepsilon_{ij}\) and let the agent, \(i\), choose the one with the highest utility, and the same machinery covers a whole menu of options — candidates in an election, brands on a shelf, foreign policy options. The binary model is just the two-option case of that; we’ll build the general version — several alternatives, McFadden’s derivation, and what the error assumption buys and costs — in the choice model weeks later in the semester.


This is what makes the link function not arbitrary: \(F\) is the CDF of the latent error. Different assumptions about \(\varepsilon\) give different link functions.

\(\varepsilon \sim N(0,1)\) \(\longrightarrow\) probit, \(F = \Phi\)
\(\varepsilon \sim \text{Logistic}(0,1)\) \(\longrightarrow\) logit, \(F = \Lambda\)
\(\varepsilon \sim \text{Gumbel}\) \(\longrightarrow\) complementary log-log

Figure 2 illustrates this for a normal (probit) error. Think of the latent variable \(y^* = x\beta + \varepsilon\) as a distribution sitting over the real line, centered at \(x\beta\), with the threshold fixed at zero; \(Pr(y=1)\) is the share of it lying to the right of zero. Raising \(x\beta\) slides the whole distribution rightward, so more of it clears the threshold and \(Pr(y=1)\) rises; lowering \(x\beta\) slides it left. Imagine \(x\beta\) at values ranging across the x-axis, and that share accumulates from zero up to one — which is exactly what a CDF does, and why \(F\) is one. So the link is no arbitrary sigmoid: choosing \(F\) is choosing a distribution for the error.2


code
# TOP: the latent bell y* = xb + e ~ N(xb, 1); the shaded area past the fixed
# threshold at 0 is Pr(y=1). That area = 1 - Phi(-xb) = Phi(xb) (standardize --
# the threshold sits -xb SDs from the mean). BOTTOM: plot each shaded area
# against xb and it traces the CDF Phi, so the shaded area up top IS the CDF
# height below. Drawn for a normal error (probit); logit tells the same story.
xb_vals <- c(-1.5, 0, 1.5)
strip   <- sprintf("xb = %g   (shaded area = %.2f)", xb_vals, pnorm(xb_vals))

dens_df <- tibble(xb    = rep(xb_vals, each = 400),
                  ystar = rep(seq(-5, 5, length.out = 400), times = 3)) %>%
  mutate(dens  = dnorm(ystar, mean = xb, sd = 1),
         facet = factor(sprintf("xb = %g   (shaded area = %.2f)", xb, pnorm(xb)),
                        levels = strip))
shaded <- filter(dens_df, ystar > 0)

# Top row: the three bells, shaded area past the threshold = Pr(y=1) = Phi(xb).
p_bells <- ggplot(dens_df, aes(ystar, dens)) +
  geom_area(data = shaded, fill = bu_lightgreen, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(color = bu_green, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +           # the fixed threshold
  facet_wrap(~ facet, nrow = 1) +
  labs(title = "Top: the shaded area past the threshold is Pr(y=1) = Phi(xb)",
       x = expression(y^"*"~"(latent variable)"), y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

# Bottom row: those areas plotted against xb -- this traces the CDF, the link.
cdf_df <- tibble(xb = seq(-5, 5, length.out = 400), p = pnorm(xb))
marks  <- tibble(xb = xb_vals, p = pnorm(xb_vals))

p_cdf <- ggplot(cdf_df, aes(xb, p)) +
  geom_line(color = bu_green, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_segment(data = marks, aes(x = xb, xend = xb, y = 0, yend = p),
               color = bu_grey, linetype = "dotted") +        # read up from xb
  geom_segment(data = marks, aes(x = -5, xend = xb, y = p, yend = p),
               color = bu_grey, linetype = "dotted") +        # ... across to the height
  geom_point(data = marks, aes(xb, p), color = bu_black, size = 2) +
  geom_text(data = marks, aes(xb, p, label = sprintf("(%g, %.2f)", xb, p)),
            vjust = -0.9, hjust = -0.05, size = 3.1, color = bu_black) +
  labs(title = "Bottom: plot each shaded area against xb and you trace the CDF -- the link F",
       x = expression(x*beta), y = expression(Phi(x*beta))) +
  theme_minimal()

p_bells / p_cdf








Figure 2





Look at the two panels together. Each curve’s shaded area is a single number — the probability past the threshold — and computing it is one standardization: the bell is \(N(x\beta, 1)\), so the threshold at \(0\) sits \(-x\beta\) standard deviations from the mean, and the area to its right is \(1 - \Phi(-x\beta) = \Phi(x\beta)\). That is the whole translation onto the CDF. Take the lefthand bell-curve, \(x\beta = -1.5\): the threshold is \(1.5\) standard deviations above the mean, so only the far tail clears it — about 0.07 of the mass — which is \(\Phi(-1.5)\), and that is exactly the height of the CDF at \(x\beta = -1.5\) in the bottom panel. The middle bell splits at the mean (area \(0.5\)), the right bell clears most of the threshold (about 0.93), and plotting those three areas against \(x\beta\) traces the whole sigmoid: the CDF is the shaded area, accumulated as \(x\beta\) moves. Keep these PDFs in mind because the topic returns in the marginal-effects section below, where we use the PDF’s height rather than its area.
Examine the figure a second time through the lens of \(Pr(\varepsilon_i > -x_i\beta)\) from the latent variable motivation above: the shaded area is that probability — the chance the idiosyncratic \(\varepsilon_i\) clears the bar the systematic part sets at \(-x_i\beta\). For the lefthand bell, \(x_i\beta = -1.5\), so the bar sits at \(-x_i\beta = +1.5\): reaching \(y=1\) takes a large favorable shock, \(\varepsilon_i > 1.5\), which happens only rarely. For the righthand bell, \(x_i\beta = +1.5\), so the bar drops to \(-x_i\beta = -1.5\): almost any \(\varepsilon_i\) clears it, and it is now \(y=0\) that would need a large unfavorable shock, \(\varepsilon_i < -1.5\). Raising \(x_i\beta\) slides the bar left — from \(+1.5\) toward \(-1.5\), asking less and less of the error, the same movement as the shaded area growing from 0.07 to 0.93.

title: Binary Response Models
section: A nonlinear model for binary data
text:
A nonlinear model for binary data
\(y\) is binary, and we’ve established that the linear model is not appropriate. The observed variable \(y\) is binomial (iid) — it takes the value 1 with probability \(\pi_i\) and 0 with probability \(1-\pi_i\):
\[
y \sim f_{\text{binomial}}(\pi_i)
\]
\[
y_i = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{with probability } \pi_i \\ 0, & \text{with probability } 1-\pi_i \end{cases}
\]
Two features run through everything below. First, the model has two parts — one for the ones and one for the zeros — and they are mirror images of each other: whatever we write for \(\pi_i\) when \(y=1\), we write for \(1-\pi_i\) when \(y=0\). Second, both parts go through the same link function \(F\), which turns the linear predictor \(x_i\beta\) into a probability:
\[
\pi_i = F(x_i\beta), \qquad 1-\pi_i = 1 - F(x_i\beta)
\]
So using the link, \(F(x_i\beta)\) is the probability of a one, and \(1 - F(x_i\beta)\) is the probability of a zero. Keep that symmetry in mind because this is the shape of every likelihood equation that follows.

title: Binary Response Models
text:
The binomial likelihood
Write the binomial density (the probability of a single observation):
\[
Pr(y_i = y \mid \pi_i) = \pi_i^{y_i}(1-\pi_i)^{1-y_i}
\]
Read this as the two-part model in one line: when \(y_i = 1\) it returns \(\pi_i\); when \(y_i = 0\) it returns \(1-\pi_i\). The exponents are just switches that select the right piece.
Write the joint probability of the data as a likelihood — the product over \(n\) iid observations, read as a function of the unknown \(\pi\):
\[
\mathcal{L}(\pi \mid y) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\pi_i^{y_i}(1-\pi_i)^{1-y_i}
\]
Take the log of that likelihood, which turns the product into a sum:
\[
\ln\mathcal{L}(\pi \mid y) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[y_i \ln \pi_i + (1-y_i)\ln(1-\pi_i)\right]
\]
We now have a generic and flexible log-likelihood function appropriate for binary response variables.

title: Binary Response Models
text:
Parameterize the model
So far \(\pi_i\) is just “the probability of a one.” To make it a model — to let covariates shape that probability — we parameterize it: we make \(\pi_i\) a function of some variables and their slope effects, \(x\beta\). This step is worth pausing on, because parameterizing a distribution’s parameter will be a recurring act all semester and may be a new idea. Every distribution we meet has a parameter (here \(\pi\) for the binomial; for the Poisson it will be a rate \(\lambda\)). “Parameterizing” means writing that parameter as a function of covariates — the systematic component of the model — so that the data can move the probability around:
\[
\pi_i = F(x\beta)
\]
Substituting into the log-likelihood gives the binomial log-likelihood function in terms of \(\beta\), which is what we actually estimate:
\[
\ln\mathcal{L}(\beta \mid y, X) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[y_i \ln F(x_i\beta) + (1-y_i)\ln(1-F(x_i\beta))\right]
\]
But we still need to fill in \(F\), the link function.

title: Binary Response Models
text:
The link function
We parameterized \(\pi_i = F(x\beta)\), and now we need to choose an \(F\) that maps the linear prediction onto \(\pi_i\) — the probability of a one. The systematic component \(x_i\beta\) can range over \([-\infty, +\infty]\), but a probability cannot — so \(F\) has to do two things:

map the whole real line onto \([0,1]\), so our prediction \(\widehat{\pi}_i\) is a genuine probability;
do it smoothly and monotonically — a sigmoid — so more \(x\beta\) always means more probability.

Any sigmoid CDF satisfies the bounds; the two we use most commonly are the standard normal (probit) and the logistic (logit). Recall that the CDF we choose for the link also characterizes the distribution of the latent errors per the discussion above.
\[
Pr(y_i = 1 \mid X) = \Phi(x_i\beta) \qquad \text{(probit)}
\]
\[
Pr(y_i = 1 \mid X) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x_i\beta}} \qquad \text{(logit)}
\]






Important Concept



The link function maps the linear prediction onto the sigmoid probability space and obeys the bounds \([0,1]\). Choosing the link is choosing a distribution for the latent error.


This is an important general idea to remember going forward. The link is a translator between two number lines, one for \(x\beta\) (the linear prediction) and one for \(\pi\) (the probability we actually want). Pick a value on the \(x\beta\) axis, read up to the curve, read across — that’s \(F(x\beta)\). And note what “sliding” means here: the curve itself is fixed and never moves; a change in \(x\beta\) just slides the predicted point along it — left for less, right for more. Every predicted probability in the model is from this one curve.


code
# The two CDFs as translators from the linear predictor to a probability,
# with a few (xb, pi) pairs marked on the logit curve.
xb <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 400)
curve_df <- tibble(xb = xb, logit = plogis(xb), probit = pnorm(xb))

marks <- tibble(xb = c(-2, 0, 2)) %>% mutate(pi = plogis(xb))

ggplot(curve_df, aes(xb, logit)) +
  geom_line(color = bu_green, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = probit), color = bu_lightgreen, linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_segment(data = marks,
               aes(x = xb, xend = xb, y = 0, yend = pi),
               color = bu_grey, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_segment(data = marks,
               aes(x = -5, xend = xb, y = pi, yend = pi),
               color = bu_grey, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_point(data = marks, aes(xb, pi), color = bu_black, size = 2) +
  geom_text(data = marks,
            aes(xb, pi, label = sprintf("(%g, %.2f)", xb, pi)),
            vjust = -0.8, hjust = -0.05, size = 3.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 3.5, y = 0.6, label = "logit~(Lambda)", parse = TRUE, color = bu_green) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = 0.95, label = "probit~(Phi)", parse = TRUE, color = bu_black) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.05)) +
  labs(title = "Link function as translator: from linear predictor to probability",
       x = expression(x*beta~"(linear prediction)"),
       y = expression(pi == F(x*beta))) +
  theme_minimal()








Figure 3











Which link to choose?



It’s also worth pointing out that in most (nearly all) social science applications, the choice of link function is inconsequential, particularly between logit and probit. As you can see, the differences lie mainly in the tails; logit has fatter tails, so more probability at the extremes. But the differences are small and in empirical settings, mostly unimportant. As we’ll see in a couple of weeks, we can select other link functions that have different properties that may more closely characterize the distribution of \(y\) and our expectations about \(\varepsilon\).

title: Binary Response Models
text:
Probit and logit log-likelihoods
Filling \(F\) into the parameterized log-likelihood gives the model we actually estimate. This is the workhorse log-likelihood, and choosing \(F\) fills in the specific model. Writing each one out makes the two-part structure concrete: the link sits inside the \(y=1\) term, and one minus the link sits inside the \(y=0\) term.
The probit uses the standard normal CDF \(\Phi\) as the link:
\[
\ln\mathcal{L}(\beta \mid y) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[\, y_i \ln \Phi(x_i\beta) + (1-y_i)\ln\big(1 - \Phi(x_i\beta)\big)\,\Big]
\]
The logit uses the logistic CDF, \(\Lambda(x_i\beta) = \tfrac{1}{1+e^{-x_i\beta}}\):
\[
\ln\mathcal{L}(\beta \mid y) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\{\, y_i \ln\!\left(\frac{1}{1+e^{-x_i\beta}}\right) + (1-y_i)\ln\!\left[\,1 - \frac{1}{1+e^{-x_i\beta}}\,\right] \right\}
\]
As we did earlier, think of the two terms as the two outcomes, zero and one. The first term is the contribution of the cases where \(y=1\) — the probability the model assigns to a one, \(F(x_i\beta)\). The second term is the contribution of the cases where \(y=0\) — the probability it assigns to a zero, \(1 - F(x_i\beta)\). Choosing the link changes what sits inside the parentheses; it does not change that two-part structure. The probit puts \(\Phi\) in both slots, the logit puts \(\Lambda\) in both slots, and any other binary-response model we write does the same thing with its own \(F\).
That is the likelihood. Maximizing it — taking its derivatives and climbing to the \(\beta\) that makes the observed data most probable — is the topic for the next couple of weeks. For now, we’ll estimate the model and interpret it.

title: Binary Response Models
text:
Predicted probabilities
Predicted probabilities are the most commonly reported quantities of interest for binary response models. For the logit, the predicted probability is3
\[
\widehat{Pr}(y=1\mid X) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x\widehat\beta}},
\]
and for the probit the probability \(y=1\) is:
\[
\widehat{Pr}(y=1\mid X) = \Phi(x\widehat\beta).
\]
In both cases we are doing the same thing — transforming the linear prediction \(x\widehat\beta\) through the link function so it maps onto the \([0,1]\) probability space.
The figure below does this for democracy. These are at-means (adjusted) predictions — democracy varies across its range while the other covariates are held at representative values (the mode for the binary covariates, the median for the skewed capability ratio). We’ll revisit prediction methods specifically in the context of nonlinear models in the coming weeks.


code
# At-means (adjusted) predictions: democracy varies across its range; the other
# x-variables are held at representative values -- the mode for the binary
# covariates (border, ally), the median for skewed capability ratio.
# (datagrid's default would hold numerics at their mean; I set them
# to the mode/median to address skewness)
modal <- function(x) as.numeric(names(which.max(table(x)))) #function to find mode - R lacks such a function

preds_dem <- predictions(
  m_logit,
  newdata = datagrid(deml   = seq(-10, 10, length.out = 21), #functions from "marginaleffects" library to generate data for predictions
                     border = modal(dp$border),
                     ally   = modal(dp$ally),
                     lncaprat = median(dp$lncaprat, na.rm = TRUE))
)

ggplot(preds_dem, aes(deml, estimate)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high),
              fill = bu_green, alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(color = bu_green, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Predicted Pr(dispute = 1) across democracy",
       x = "minimum dyad democracy (Polity)",
       y = "Pr(y = 1)") +
  theme_minimal()









The prediction plot indicates that for a non-bordering, non-allied dyad at median capabilities, the probability of a militarized dispute is about 0.048 when the two states are maximally autocratic (minimum democracy \(=-10\)), and about 0.012 when they are maximally democratic (\(=+10\)). So moving a dyad from fully autocratic to fully democratic cuts its predicted chance of a dispute to roughly a quarter of what it was.

title: Binary Response Models
text:
Marginal effects
Start with the linear model, where this is easy and familiar. The marginal effect of \(x_k\) — the change in \(\widehat y\) for a one-unit change in \(x_k\) — is just \(\widehat\beta_k\):
\[
\frac{\partial \widehat y}{\partial x_k} = \frac{\partial\, x\widehat\beta}{\partial x_k} = \widehat\beta_k.
\]
It is constant — the same at every value of \(x\).


code
me_line <- tibble(x = seq(0, 10, 0.1), y = 2 * x)

ggplot(me_line, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line(color = bu_green, linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("segment", x = 5,  xend = 5,  y = 0, yend = 10, color = "red") +
  annotate("segment", x = 10, xend = 10, y = 0, yend = 20, color = "red") +
  annotate("text", x = 3.5, y = 16, label = "y = 2x") +
  labs(title = "A linear marginal effect is constant", x = "x", y = "y") +
  theme_minimal()









The effect of \(x\) on \(y\) here is 2 — the same at \(x=5\) as at \(x=10\). The nonlinear model breaks that. Because the prediction runs through the curve \(F\), the marginal effect depends on where on the curve we are — that is, on where \(x\widehat\beta\) sits with respect to that curve:
\[
\frac{\partial Pr(y=1)}{\partial x_k} = \frac{\partial F(x\beta)}{\partial x\beta}\cdot\frac{\partial x\beta}{\partial x_k} = f(x\beta)\,\widehat{\beta}_k,
\]
where the derivative of the CDF \(F\) is its PDF \(f\). So the marginal effect is \(\widehat\beta_k\) weighted by the height of the PDF at \(x\widehat\beta\) — large where the density is tall, small where it is flat.






Important Concept



The effect of \(x\) on \(Pr(y=1)\) is not constant. It is largest where the latent PDF is densest — for probit and logit, that’s near \(x\beta=0\), i.e., where \(Pr(y=1) \approx 0.5\). Near the floor (0) or ceiling (1), the same \(\widehat{\beta}\) moves the probability hardly at all.


Take a look at the next figure — it shows the logit CDF with tangent line slopes at three different points. The link function is a single fixed sigmoid; the marginal effect at any point is its slope there. In the middle, the curve is steep, so a change in \(x\beta\) moves the probability a lot; out in the tails it is nearly flat, so the same change barely moves it. Where a given case sits on the curve is set by its own values of the \(x\) variables — as they increase, it slides right toward the steep middle; as they decrease, it slides left into the flat tail. That is why one coefficient can deliver a large effect for one case and a tiny one for another: same \(\widehat\beta\), different place on the curve.






Two important asides on marginal effects



First, note the symmetry of the CDF (true for logistic and normal) — the slopes in the tails are the same even though the values of \(x\beta\) would be different from one another, as would the predicted probabilities. It is also the case that the maximum slope in the middle at zero (0.25) is the maximum height of the logit PDF — we’ll see the two side by side shortly. This implies that the maximum marginal effect of any \(x_k\) variable in a logit model is \(0.25\,\widehat\beta_k\). You’ll see this illustrated below.
Second, as indicated above, a change in any \(x_k\) will shift the prediction on the CDF. Changing the value of a control variable will change the predicted probability even if the variable of interest stays the same. In a couple of weeks, we’ll return to this — the inherent interactivity of nonlinear models, which Nagler describes as being “‘interactive’ in all of their variables” and inherent to the specification (Nagler 1994, 1991; Ai and Norton 2003; Berry, DeMeritt, and Esarey 2010).




code
# The marginal effect of a covariate is the SLOPE of the link at the point where
# a case sits. For the logit that slope is the density lambda(xb), which works out
# to Lambda(xb)*(1-Lambda(xb)) = Pr(1)*Pr(0) (derived in "Logit marginal effects"
# below):
# tallest in the middle (0.25 at xb = 0, where Pr = .5), flat in the tails. A
# case's other covariates set WHERE on the curve it sits -- raise them and it
# slides toward the steep middle, lower them and it slides into the flat tail.
# Same coefficient, different effect.
sig <- tibble(xb = seq(-6, 6, length.out = 400), p = plogis(xb))

pts <- tibble(xb = c(-3, 0, 3)) %>%          # three positions on the curve
  mutate(p = plogis(xb), slope = p * (1 - p))

d <- 1.1                                      # half-length of each tangent, in xb units
tangents <- pts %>%
  mutate(x0 = xb - d, x1 = xb + d,
         y0 = p - slope * d, y1 = p + slope * d)

ggplot(sig, aes(xb, p)) +
  geom_line(color = bu_green, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_segment(data = tangents, aes(x = x0, xend = x1, y = y0, yend = y1),
               color = bu_black, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = pts, aes(xb, p), color = bu_black, size = 2) +
  geom_text(data = pts, aes(xb, p, label = sprintf("slope = %.2f", slope)),
            vjust = -1.3, size = 3.3) +
  annotate("segment", x = -3.3, xend = 3.3, y = -0.10, yend = -0.10,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "cm"), ends = "both"), color = bu_black) +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = -0.16, size = 3, color = bu_black,
           label = "a case's other covariates slide it along the curve") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.18, 1.08)) +
  labs(title = "The marginal effect is the slope of the link -- steepest in the middle",
       x = expression(x*beta), y = expression(pi == Lambda(x*beta))) +
  theme_minimal()








Figure 4





For the democratic-peace data this is why the average marginal effects below are quite small: disputes are rare, so most dyads sit far out on the flat lefthand tail, where even a relatively large coefficient moves the probability only a little.

Logit marginal effects
For the logit, the PDF \(\lambda\) has a particularly clean form. Working it through:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \Lambda(x\beta)}{\partial x_k}
&= \lambda(x\beta)\,\widehat\beta_k \\
&= \frac{e^{x\beta}}{(1+e^{x\beta})^2}\,\widehat\beta_k \\
&= \frac{e^{x\beta}}{1+e^{x\beta}}\cdot\frac{1}{1+e^{x\beta}}\,\widehat\beta_k \\
&= \Lambda(x\beta)\big(1-\Lambda(x\beta)\big)\,\widehat\beta_k.
\end{aligned}
\]
Looking at the last line above, the marginal effect is the probability of a one times the probability of a zero times \(\widehat\beta_k\). That product \(\Lambda(1-\Lambda)\) is largest when \(\Lambda = 0.5\), where it is \(0.5\times0.5 = 0.25\). So the largest marginal effect any covariate can have in a logit is \(0.25\,\widehat\beta_k\).
In the democratic-peace model, the coefficient on democracy is about -0.07. So the largest effect a one-unit change in democracy can have on the probability of a dispute is one-quarter of that — about -0.0175 — and that only near \(Pr(y=1)=0.5\), which for these rare-event data almost never happens.


Probit marginal effects
The probit works the same way, with the standard normal PDF \(\phi\) in place of \(\lambda\):
\[
\frac{\partial \Phi(x\beta)}{\partial x_k} = \phi(x\beta)\,\widehat\beta_k.
\]
The standard normal density peaks at \(x\beta = 0\), where \(\phi(0) = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \approx 0.4\). So the maximum marginal effect of any covariate in a probit is about \(0.4\,\widehat\beta_k\).
Put the two link functions side by side to see where \(0.25\) and \(0.4\) come from — and to tie the marginal effect back to the density we started with.


code
# Each link's PDF is the slope of its CDF, and the PDF's peak (at xb = 0) is the
# largest marginal-effect weight: 0.25 for the logit, 0.399 for the probit.
# Colors match fig-mapping: logit = green (solid), probit = light green (dashed).
z    <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 400)
dens <- tibble(z = z,
               logit_cdf  = plogis(z), logit_pdf  = dlogis(z),
               probit_cdf = pnorm(z),  probit_pdf = dnorm(z))

ggplot(dens, aes(z)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = logit_cdf),  color = bu_green,      linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = probit_cdf), color = bu_lightgreen, linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(aes(y = logit_pdf),  color = bu_green,      linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = probit_pdf), color = bu_lightgreen, linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.25,   color = bu_green,      linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.3989, color = bu_lightgreen, linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = -4.8, y = 0.28, hjust = 0, size = 3, color = bu_green,
           label = "logit PDF peak = 0.25") +
  annotate("text", x = -4.8, y = 0.42, hjust = 0, size = 3, color = bu_black,
           label = "probit PDF peak = 0.399") +
  annotate("text", x = 3.4,  y = 0.96, size = 3, color = bu_black, label = "CDF = the link") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.15, y = 0.33, size = 3, color = bu_black, label = "PDF = its slope") +
  labs(title = "The link's slope is its PDF; the PDF's peak is the largest marginal effect",
       x = expression(x*beta), y = "link (CDF) and its slope (PDF)") +
  theme_minimal()








Figure 5





The PDF under each S-curve is its slope — the density \(f\) — the very weight from Figure 4, now shown for both links. Its peak sits at \(x\beta = 0\): \(0.25\) for the logit, \(0.399\) for the probit. And for the probit the plot is the normal bell curve from Figure 2, whose area past the threshold gave us \(Pr(y=1)\). There we read the model off the density’s area; here we read the marginal effect off its height. Same density, two jobs.
In practice we rarely report the maximum; we report the average marginal effect — the effect computed for each case in the sample and averaged across all of them. That’s a quantity-of-interest method we develop fully later, but here is the average marginal effect for the logit:


code
ames <- avg_slopes(m_logit)

ames %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  dplyr::select(term, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Average marginal effects, logit")

Looking at these effects, we can say the average marginal effect of the minimum democracy score is about -0.0029: averaging over every dyad in the sample, raising the lower democracy score by one point lowers the predicted probability of a militarized dispute by about that much — roughly three in a thousand. It is small for the reason the callout gave: disputes are rare, so these data sit far out on the flat tail of the logistic curve, where even a genuine effect moves the probability only a little. Shared border, by contrast, carries the largest average marginal effect in the model, about 0.046 — contiguity raises the average predicted probability of a dispute by four or five percentage points.

title: Binary Response Models
text:
Logit odds and log-odds
The logit has one more interpretation that the probit lacks, and it can be a useful one. The odds of an event are the probability it happens over the probability it doesn’t:
\[
\Omega(X) = \frac{Pr(y=1)}{1-Pr(y=1)} = \frac{\Lambda(X\beta)}{1-\Lambda(X\beta)}.
\]
Take logs, and the log-odds turn out to be exactly linear in \(X\):
\[
\ln\Omega(X) = X\beta,
\]
so \(\partial \ln\Omega / \partial x_k = \widehat\beta_k\), constant. This is why a logit coefficient is sometimes just called “the logit” — it is the change in the log-odds for a one-unit change in \(x_k\).
To read a coefficient on this scale, take it at face value. The coefficient on shared border is about 1.04, so moving border from 0 to 1 adds about 1.04 to the log-odds of a dispute — and it adds the same amount whatever the other covariates are. Democracy’s coefficient is about -0.07; being negative, each one-point rise in the minimum democracy score subtracts about 0.07 from the log-odds. Additive and constant — that is the appeal of the log-odds scale. The catch is that no one has much intuition for a log-odds, which is why we usually exponentiate back to odds.

Odds ratios
Log-odds are linear but not very intuitive. Exponentiating gets us back to odds, and the ratio of the odds at \(x_k+1\) versus at \(x_k\) is simply
\[
\frac{\Omega(x_k+1)}{\Omega(x_k)} = e^{\widehat\beta_k}.
\]
The change need not be one unit; for a change of \(\delta\) it’s \(e^{\widehat\beta_k \delta}\). Most usefully,
\[100\cdot(e^{\widehat\beta_k}-1)\]
is the percentage change in the odds for a one-unit change in \(x_k\) — a summary that doesn’t depend on the values of the other \(X\) variables.
For example, the logit coefficient on shared border is about 1.04. Exponentiating that coefficient gives roughly 2.82 — so sharing a border multiplies the odds of a dispute by about that factor, a 182% increase in the odds.
Democracy runs the other way. Its coefficient is about -0.07, so exponentiating gives about 0.932 — each one-point rise in the lower democracy score multiplies the odds of a dispute by that factor, a -7% change. The minus sign carries straight through to the odds: more democracy, lower odds of conflict.

title: Binary Response Models
text:
Footnotes


A probability mass function puts a probability on each value a discrete variable can take: each value has some assigned probability, and these probabilities sum to one. A probability density function describes a continuous variable, where any single value has probability zero — there are uncountably many of them, so none can carry positive probability. The density \(f(x)\) is not a probability but a rate (probability per unit of \(x\)); you get an actual probability only by integrating it over a range — the area under the curve between two points. Hence mass at a point, density over an interval.↩︎
I used Claude Code to generate Figures 2 and 4 in these slides.↩︎
The logit probability is just as often written as \(\Lambda(x\beta) = \frac{e^{x\beta}}{1+e^{x\beta}}\), but it’s the same function. To see how, multiply the top and bottom of \(\frac{1}{1+e^{-x\beta}}\) by \(e^{x\beta}\): the top becomes \(e^{x\beta}\), and the bottom becomes \(e^{x\beta}\left(1+e^{-x\beta}\right) = e^{x\beta}+1\), since \(e^{x\beta}e^{-x\beta}=e^{0}=1\). So \(\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x\beta}} = \dfrac{e^{x\beta}}{1+e^{x\beta}}\).↩︎

title: MLE Syllabus
text:
Seminar Description
This 4 credit hour seminar is a survey of maximum likelihood methods and their applications to empirical political questions. It presumes students have a detailed and intuitive knowledge of least squares, probability theory, basic skills in scalar and matrix algebra, and a basic understanding of calculus. The course will deal mainly in understanding the principles of maximum likelihood estimation, under what conditions we move away from least squares, and what particular models are appropriate given observed data. The seminar will focus on application and interpretation of ML models and linking theory to statistical models. The course emphasizes coding and data viz in R.
The class meets one time per week for three hours. My office hours are designed to be homework help hours where I’ll work in the grad lab with any of you who are working on the exercises. The most productive pathway for this class is for you to get in the habit of working together, and those office hours are a good time for this.

title: MLE Syllabus
text:
Course Purpose
This seminar fulfills the advanced quantitative methods requirement in the Ph.D. curriculum. The method of maximum likelihood underlies a majority of quantitative models in Political Science; this class teaches students to be astute consumers of such models, and how to implement and interpret ML models. These are crucial skills for dissertations in Political Science, and for producing publishable quantitative research.

title: MLE Syllabus
text:
Learning Objectives
Students will encounter an array of maximum likelihood models in this course. By the end of the course, students will have mastered the theory of maximum likelihood sufficient to write and program likelihood functions in ; they will be able to choose, estimate, and interpret appropriate models, model specifications, and model evaluation tools given their data; and they will be able to produce sophisticated quantities of interest (e.g. predicted probabilities, expected values, confidence intervals) via a variety of techniques including simulation and end point transformation. Students will also be able to present model findings verbally and graphically.

title: MLE Syllabus
text:
Reading
The reading material for the course is important because it often demonstrates application of various MLE models; seeing how folks apply these and how they motivate their applications is really informative, something you cannot miss. We often won’t directly discuss the readings, but don’t let that imply they’re not important. If I get the sense we’re not keeping up with reading, expect the syllabus to change to incorporate quizzes or other accountability measures.
Reading for the course will consist of several books and articles (listed by week below). The books listed below also have Amazon links - you’ll find most of these cheaper used online.

Required

Box-Steffensmeier, Janet and Jones, Brad. 2004. Event History Modeling. Cambridge. ISBN 0521546737
J. Scott Long. 1997. Regression Models for Categorical and Limited Dependent Variables. Sage Publications Inc. ISBN 0803973748
Ward, Michael D. and John S. Ahlquist. 2018 Maximum Likelihood for Social Science. Cambridge. ISBN 978-1316636824.



Recommended
Useful, but not required (though some required reading in the first one):

Gary King. 1998. Unifying Political Methodology. University of Michigan Press. ISBN 0472085549


Gary King’s book is regarded as seminal in developing ML applications in political science. Scott Long’s is a similarly accessible treatment of a host of ML models and applications (and the Stata book is a great applied companion). Together, these two books are probably the most important on the syllabus as they are both accessible, but comprehensive and technical enough to be useful. Ward and Ahlquist’s book is a newer overview of applied ML in a political science setting. Box-Steffensmeier and Jones is a thorough and accessible treatment of hazard models in a variety of empirical settings.


Additional Resources
Other useful books include:

Cameron, A. Colin and Trivedi, Pravin K. 1998. Regression Analysis of Count Data. Cambridge. ISBN 0521635675
Maddala, Gregory. 1983. Limited Dependent and Qualitative Variables in Econometrics. Cambridge. ISBN 0521338255
Paul D Allison - Event History Analysis : Regression for Longitudinal Event Data. Sage Publications Inc. ISBN 0803920555
Tim Futing Liao - Interpreting Probability Models : Logit, Probit, and Other Generalized Linear Models. Sage Publications Inc. ISBN 0803949995
John H Aldrich and Forrest D Nelson - Linear Probability, Logit, and Probit Models. Sage Publications Inc. ISBN 0803921330
Fred C Pampel - Logistic Regression : A Primer. Sage Publications Inc. ISBN 0761920102
Vani Kant Borooah - Logit and Probit : Ordered and Multinomial Models. Sage Publications Inc. ISBN 0761922423
Scott R Eliason - Maximum Likelihood Estimation : Logic and Practice. Sage Publications Inc. ISBN 0803941072
Richard Breen - Regression Models : Censored, Sample Selected, or Truncated Data. Sage Publications Inc. ISBN 0803957106
Krishnan Namboodiri - Matrix Algebra : An Introduction. ISBN 0803920520

title: MLE Syllabus
text:
Course Requirements and Grades
The seminar requires the following:

Problem sets - 60% total
Mechanism papers - 40%

Please note that all written assignments must be submitted as PDFs either compiled in LaTeX or in R markdown (Quarto).
You’ll complete a series of problem sets, mostly applied. How many will depend on how things move along during the term (roughly 8-10). Regarding the problem sets - the work you turn in for the problem sets should clearly be your own, but I urge you to work together - doing so is a great way to learn and to overcome problems.
The mechanism papers are a series of three short papers you’ll write during the semester aimed at learning to identify and describe causal mechanisms, then at producing a causal mechanism. More on these early in the term.
A word about completeness - attempt everything. To receive a passing grade in the course, you must finish all elements of the course, so all problem sets, all exams, papers, etc. To complete an element, you must at least attempt all parts of the element - so if a problem set has 10 problems, you must attempt all 10 or the assignment is incomplete, you’ve not completed every element of the course, and you cannot pass. title: MLE Syllabus
text:
Course Policies

Attendance
Attendance is expected, and is essential if you’re to succeed in this class.


Academic Integrity
Ideas are the currency in academic exchange, so acknowledging where ideas come from is important. Acknowledging the sources of ideas also helps us identify an idea’s lineage which can be important for understanding how that line of thought has developed, and toward promoting future growth. As graduate students, you should have a good understanding of academic honesty and best practices. Here are details of Binghamton’s honesty policy.


Artificial Intelligence and Coding Tools
Generative AI can act as an incredible accelerator for research, for coding and data management in particular. Such tools are only as useful as your own mastery of coding, data management, and modeling.
Do you need to be able to write code when AI can do it for you? Yes. Three reasons:

Understanding. Code and the act of coding are the windows to seeing and understanding data, models, and predictions — how data produce models, which in turn produce predictions. Code is an explicit connection between a data matrix and a model, and facilitates your understanding of the what the model produces. AI can’t hand you that understanding; you build it by doing the work yourself.
Criticism. AI will produce code. If you can code, you can read it, critique it, and evaluate its output to judge whether it’s right. If you can’t code, you can’t do any of that — you’re left trusting output you have no way to check.
Inquiry. If you don’t understand the code, you probably don’t understand the data and the model, and you’ll not write a very good query to the AI in the first place. AI is only as good as its user. You should always know things the AI does not, in terms of your argument, your data, your model, and your code.

So here is the policy for this course. Do not use generative AI to produce code. If you get stuck coding, you may use AI to get unstuck - this is equivalent to consulting “stackexchange” or “stackoverflow” to solve code problems and get unstuck. Anytime you consult AI, you must cite and annotate it specifically: what you asked, why you asked it, and which parts of your code came from the AI. To this end, expect assessment where I ask you to show that you understand the data, code, models, and predictions you are producing. A bot can’t fake that understanding.
You should not use generative AI tools for writing in this course. Learning to express your ideas about politics, about causal relations, about data and models, and explaining your findings are core skills for the Ph.D. Please learn to do these things without any use of generative AI.

title: Prediction Methods in the Linear Model
section: The ML standard error of the linear prediction
text:
The ML standard error of the linear prediction
The most direct measure of uncertainty is the standard error of the linear prediction \(X\widehat\beta\). It comes from the variance–covariance matrix of \(\widehat\beta\):
\[
\mathrm{Var}(X\widehat\beta) = \mathbf{X}\,\mathbf{V}\,\mathbf{X}',
\]
an \(N \times N\) matrix, where \(\mathbf{V} = \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\widehat\beta) =\) vcov(m1). Its diagonal holds the variances of the \(N\) predictions, so
\[
se(X\widehat\beta) = \sqrt{\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{X}\,\mathbf{V}\,\mathbf{X}')},
\]
an \(N \times 1\) vector. In the MLE class this \(\mathbf{V}\) is the \((-H)^{-1}\) from the likelihood notes; in OLS it is the familiar \(\widehat\sigma^2 (X'X)^{-1}\). Same formula, and it produces exactly the standard error predict() reports. Here it is by hand, on the at-means protest grid, checked against predict():


code
# design matrix for the at-means grid (protest varies, others held)
Xg <- model.matrix(~ lagRA + civilwar + lagprotest + p1 + p2 + loggdp, data = oosdata)
V  <- vcov(m1)

xb     <- as.vector(Xg %*% coef(m1))        # linear prediction x'b (= y-hat in OLS)
se_lin <- sqrt(diag(Xg %*% V %*% t(Xg)))    # ML SE of x'b, by hand

# check against predict()'s SE
data.frame(lagprotest = oosdata$lagprotest,
           se_byhand  = se_lin,
           se_predict = predict(m1, newdata = oosdata, se.fit = TRUE)$se.fit)[1:5, ]


  lagprotest se_byhand se_predict
1          0 0.6379299  0.6379299
2          1 0.6063378  0.6063378
3          2 0.5832546  0.5832546
4          3 0.5697154  0.5697154
5          4 0.5664052  0.5664052


They agree to machine precision: predict’s standard errors are this \(\sqrt{\mathrm{diag}(XVX')}\) computation. Please note the value of understanding basic matrix algebra for doing this. You might ask why you’d ever need to do this - some estimation packages in R do not have predict functions, or have sufficiently opaque functions that computing your own quantities is preferable.

title: Prediction Methods in the Linear Model
text:
Delta-method standard errors
When do we use the ML standard error, and when the delta method? Use the ML standard error — \(\sqrt{\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{X V X'})}\) — for the linear prediction itself, or for a quantity we can reach by transforming it: build the interval on the linear scale and map the endpoints through the link (a predicted probability from a logit or probit works this way). Use the delta method when the quantity of interest is a nonlinear function of the coefficients that we cannot reach by transforming a single linear prediction — a marginal effect that combines several coefficients, a ratio of coefficients, or a probability in a model like multinomial logit, where the quantity is not monotone in any one \(x\widehat\beta\). In the linear model, for \(\widehat y\) itself the two agree exactly, and the reason is worth seeing.






ML or delta — which, and when?



ML standard error — \(\sqrt{\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{X V X'})}\) — for the linear prediction \(x\widehat\beta\) itself, or for a quantity we reach by transforming it monotonically (build the interval on the linear scale, then map the endpoints through the link).
Delta method — for a nonlinear function of the coefficients we cannot reach that way: a marginal effect that combines several coefficients (the polynomial below), a ratio of coefficients, or a probability that is not monotone in any one \(x\widehat\beta\) (multinomial logit).
In OLS, for \(\widehat y\) the two produce the same number.


Greene (2012) gives the delta method’s general form for a transformation \(F\),
\[
\mathrm{Var}\!\left[F(X\widehat\beta)\right] = f(x'\widehat\beta)^2 \; \mathbf{x}'\,\mathbf{V}\,\mathbf{x},
\]
where \(f\) is the derivative of \(F\). In OLS the quantity of interest is the linear prediction, so \(F\) is the identity, \(f = 1\), and the delta standard error of \(\widehat y\) is just \(\sqrt{\mathbf{x}'\mathbf{V}\mathbf{x}}\) — the same se_lin we just built. In the linear model, delta and ML give the same number, because there is no nonlinear link to differentiate. In MLE, \(f\) is the link’s PDF (0.25 at the peak for the logit, 0.399 for the probit), and the two standard errors part ways.
Where the delta method earns its keep within OLS is a nonlinear function of the coefficients — a linear combination whose standard error must carry the covariances between estimates. This is not a prediction sweep; we generate the quantities of interest over protest. It is a short worked example of how we get the standard error of a linear combination, and the quadratic Polity term is the natural vehicle for it. The marginal effect of Polity is not a single coefficient but
\[
\frac{\partial \, \widehat y}{\partial \, \text{polity}} = \widehat\beta_{p1} + 2\,\widehat\beta_{p2}\,\text{polity},
\]
and its standard error carries the covariance term:
\[
se = \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\widehat\beta_{p1}) + 4\,\text{polity}^2\,\mathrm{Var}(\widehat\beta_{p2}) + 4\,\text{polity}\,\mathrm{Cov}(\widehat\beta_{p1}, \widehat\beta_{p2})}.
\]
The variances and the covariance come straight from \(\mathbf{V} =\) vcov(m1):


code
b <- coef(m1); V <- vcov(m1)

# Two small functions, each taking a Polity value p (or a whole vector of them).
# me_polity() returns the marginal effect b_p1 + 2*b_p2*p; se_polity() returns
# its delta-method standard error. Both read the coefficient vector b and the
# covariance matrix V from the two lines just above -- these are NOT passed in as
# arguments, so the functions use whatever b and V currently hold. We call each
# below on the vector `poly`, so they return one value per Polity value.
me_polity <- function(p) b["p1"] + 2*b["p2"]*p                 # marginal effect at polity = p
se_polity <- function(p) sqrt(V["p1","p1"] + 4*p^2*V["p2","p2"] +
                              4*p*V["p1","p2"])                # its delta-method SE

poly <- seq(0, 20, 2)
data.frame(polity = poly,
           marg_effect = as.numeric(me_polity(poly)),
           se          = as.numeric(se_polity(poly))) %>%
  mutate(lb = marg_effect - 1.96*se, ub = marg_effect + 1.96*se)


   polity marg_effect         se         lb        ub
1       0 -0.01601086 0.35706137 -0.7158512 0.6838294
2       2 -0.01607049 0.29739200 -0.5989588 0.5668178
3       4 -0.01613011 0.23824773 -0.4830957 0.4508354
4       6 -0.01618973 0.18014647 -0.3692768 0.3368973
5       8 -0.01624935 0.12455648 -0.2603801 0.2278813

code
# ---- MORE EFFICIENT -----------------------------------
# marginaleffects::slopes() computes this marginal effect AND its delta-method
# SE from the model object, with no hand-written covariance formula:
#
#   library(marginaleffects)
#   slopes(m1, variables = "p1", newdata = datagrid(p1 = seq(0, 20, 2)))
#
# WHY it's better: you never transcribe the "b1 + 2*b2*x" derivative or the
# variance formula, so there's nothing to get wrong -- marginaleffects
# differentiates the prediction numerically and pulls the covariances from V
# itself. The by-hand version is here so the covariance term is visible: that
# middle 4*p*Cov(b1,b2) piece is exactly what a naive SE(b1) + SE(2*b2*x) would
# miss.


Look at the output. The marginal effect of Polity hovers around zero and its interval covers zero everywhere, because neither Polity term is doing anything in this model. That is the point, not a defect: the procedure for the standard error of a linear combination is identical whether or not the effect is real — we compute it the same way for a null result and a strong one. And notice what the covariance term buys us. Dropping it — pretending \(\mathrm{Cov}(\widehat\beta_{p1}, \widehat\beta_{p2}) = 0\) — gives the wrong standard error, because in a polynomial the two coefficients are strongly correlated by construction.

title: Prediction Methods in the Linear Model
text:
Confidence intervals by end-point transformation
Either standard error can build the interval. Take the point estimate plus and minus 1.96 times the ML or the delta standard error, transforming the endpoints if the quantity is transformed:
\[
F(X\widehat\beta - 1.96\,se) \;\le\; F(X\widehat\beta) \;\le\; F(X\widehat\beta + 1.96\,se).
\]
The choice between the two matters only for a nonlinear quantity. An interval built on the linear predictor with the ML standard error and then transformed stays inside the natural bounds — a probability stays in \([0,1]\) — and comes out asymmetric. An interval built directly on the transformed quantity with the delta standard error is symmetric, and can fall outside those bounds. In OLS neither issue arises: \(F\) is the identity, so the interval is the symmetric \(\widehat y \pm 1.96\,se\) from the at-means figure, and the ML and delta standard errors are the same number to begin with. In a nonlinear model \(F\) is the link, and the difference between the two intervals is real.






Either standard error builds a confidence interval



Take the point estimate \(\pm\,1.96 \times se\) with either the ML or the delta standard error, transforming the endpoints if the quantity is transformed. The choice matters only for a nonlinear quantity: the ML interval (built on the linear scale, then transformed) stays in bounds and is asymmetric; the delta interval (built on the response) is symmetric and can leave the bounds. In OLS they coincide.

title: Prediction Methods in the Linear Model
section: Simulating the parameters — the expected value (confidence interval)
text:
Simulating the parameters — the expected value (confidence interval)
Treat \(\widehat\beta\) as the mean of a multivariate normal and \(\mathbf{V}\) as its variance, draw 10,000 coefficient vectors, and for each value of protest form the 10,000 linear predictions and take the percentiles.


code
B <- data.frame(rmvnorm(n = 10000, mean = coef(m1), sigma = vcov(m1)))
colnames(B) <- c("b0", "b_ra", "b_cw", "b_pro", "b_p1", "b_p2", "b_gdp")

sim.exp <- data.frame(lb = numeric(0), med = numeric(0), ub = numeric(0), pr = numeric(0))

for (i in seq(0, 37, 1)) {
  xbR <- quantile(B$b0 + B$b_ra*0 + B$b_cw*0 + B$b_pro*i +
                  B$b_p1*p1med + B$b_p2*p2med + B$b_gdp*gdpmed,
                  probs = c(.025, .5, .975))
  sim.exp[i + 1, 1:4] <- data.frame(t(xbR), i)
}

sim.exp %>% head()


        lb      med       ub pr
1 4.172945 5.420639 6.665929  0
2 4.475042 5.661991 6.850677  1
3 4.757268 5.904290 7.036988  2
4 5.029860 6.145498 7.259408  3
5 5.283568 6.387826 7.493155  4
6 5.516782 6.633641 7.752399  5


code
# ---- MORE EFFICIENT -----------------------------------
# Draw with MASS::mvrnorm, build all the linear predictions as one matrix
# multiply instead of looping, and skip the data.frame-row assignment:
#
#   sims <- MASS::mvrnorm(10000, coef(m1), vcov(m1))       # 10000 x k
#   grid <- seq(0, 37, 1)
#   Xg   <- model.matrix(~ lagRA + civilwar + lagprotest + p1 + p2 + loggdp,
#             data = data.frame(lagRA = 0, civilwar = 0, lagprotest = grid,
#                               p1 = p1med, p2 = p2med, loggdp = gdpmed))
#   XB   <- Xg %*% t(sims)                                 # length(grid) x 10000
#   ci   <- t(apply(XB, 1, quantile, c(.025, .5, .975)))   # one row per protest value
#
# WHY it's better: the matrix multiply replaces the loop and the fragile
# "i + 1" indexing, and building x'b from model.matrix means you never re-type
# the linear predictor by hand (where a dropped term hides). The manual loop is
# here because writing x'b out term-by-term makes it obvious what's being
# simulated.

title: Prediction Methods in the Linear Model
section: Simulating the quantity of interest — the predicted value (prediction interval)
text:
Simulating the quantity of interest — the predicted value (prediction interval)
Same draws of the parameters, but now we also add the fundamental uncertainty: for each simulated \(x\beta^{*}\) we add a disturbance draw \(\varepsilon^{*} \sim N(0, \widehat\sigma^2)\), where \(\widehat\sigma\) is the residual standard error, and take percentiles of the predicted value \(\widetilde y = x\beta^{*} + \varepsilon^{*}\).


code
sigma_hat <- sigma(m1)   # residual standard error -- the scatter around the line

sim.pred <- data.frame(lb = numeric(0), med = numeric(0), ub = numeric(0), pr = numeric(0))

for (i in seq(0, 37, 1)) {
  xstar <- B$b0 + B$b_pro*i + B$b_p1*p1med + B$b_p2*p2med + B$b_gdp*gdpmed  # binaries = 0
  ystar <- xstar + rnorm(length(xstar), mean = 0, sd = sigma_hat)          # add fundamental noise
  q <- quantile(ystar, probs = c(.025, .5, .975))
  sim.pred[i + 1, 1:4] <- data.frame(t(q), i)
}

sim.pred %>% head()


         lb      med       ub pr
1 -14.60143 5.400084 25.34124  0
2 -14.50950 5.690950 25.64214  1
3 -14.19927 6.174480 26.09840  2
4 -14.17129 5.990618 26.02624  3
5 -13.31731 6.505752 26.59697  4
6 -13.13051 6.534256 26.45667  5


Now put the two intervals on one plot, and overlay what predict() gives directly — the simulation should reproduce the analytic confidence and prediction intervals.


code
# analytic confidence and prediction intervals straight from predict()
check <- data.frame(lagprotest = oosdata$lagprotest,
  predict(m1, newdata = oosdata, interval = "confidence"),
  predict(m1, newdata = oosdata, interval = "prediction")) %>%
  rename(ci_lb = lwr, ci_ub = upr, pi_lb = lwr.1, pi_ub = upr.1)

ggplot() +
  # simulated prediction interval (wide) and confidence interval (narrow)
  geom_ribbon(data = sim.pred, aes(x = pr, ymin = lb, ymax = ub),
              fill = bu_lightgreen, alpha = .25) +
  geom_ribbon(data = sim.exp,  aes(x = pr, ymin = lb, ymax = ub),
              fill = bu_green, alpha = .35) +
  geom_line(data = sim.exp, aes(x = pr, y = med), color = bu_green, linewidth = 1) +
  # analytic checks, dashed, in dark ink so they read on the bands
  geom_line(data = check, aes(lagprotest, ci_lb), color = bu_black, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = check, aes(lagprotest, ci_ub), color = bu_black, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = check, aes(lagprotest, pi_lb), color = bu_black, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line(data = check, aes(lagprotest, pi_ub), color = bu_black, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = bu_black, linewidth = .3) +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = 11, label = "confidence interval\n(expected value)",
           hjust = 0, size = 3, color = bu_green) +
  annotate("text", x = 20, y = 26, label = "prediction interval\n(predicted value)",
           hjust = 0, size = 3, color = bu_black) +
  labs(title = "Two simulations: expected value vs. predicted value",
       subtitle = "solid/dark band = confidence interval; pale band = prediction interval; dashed/dotted = predict()",
       x = "Protests (t-1)", y = "Scarring torture") +
  theme_minimal()









The simulated bands land on the analytic ones — the dashed confidence bounds sit on the dark band, the dotted prediction bounds on the pale one. That is the payoff: the two “types of simulation” are not two techniques for the same quantity, they are two quantities. The confidence interval is our uncertainty about the average; the prediction interval is our uncertainty about a case, and it is much wider because it carries \(\widehat\sigma\).
And look where the prediction interval goes — below zero, for a variable that counts torture allegations and cannot be negative. OLS does not know scarring is a bounded count, so it puts real probability mass on impossible values. Nothing we do to the uncertainty technique fixes that; the fix is a different model, one whose link function keeps predictions non-negative (see count models in a few weeks)

title: Prediction Methods in the Linear Model
text:
Simulating combinations of binary variables
Simulation also lets us compare discrete scenarios and see the whole predicted distribution, not just a point and an interval. Here are the four combinations of restricted access and civil war, holding protest, Polity, and GDP at their medians, each as a density of simulated expected values.


code
# xb_scen() builds the simulated linear prediction for one access/war scenario.
# Its arguments are ra (restricted access, 0/1) and cw (civil war, 0/1). The
# other pieces come from the environment: the simulated coefficient columns
# B$... were drawn in the simulation chunk above, and the held medians
# promed/p1med/p2med/gdpmed in the estimation-sample chunk. It returns a full
# column of 10,000 simulated predictions. We call it four times, once per
# combination of ra and cw:
xb_scen <- function(ra, cw) {
  B$b0 + B$b_ra*ra + B$b_cw*cw + B$b_pro*promed +
  B$b_p1*p1med + B$b_p2*p2med + B$b_gdp*gdpmed
}

combos <- data.frame(ra0cw0 = xb_scen(0, 0), ra1cw0 = xb_scen(1, 0),
                     ra0cw1 = xb_scen(0, 1), ra1cw1 = xb_scen(1, 1))

ggplot(combos) +
  geom_density(aes(ra0cw0), fill = bu_green,      alpha = .3) +
  geom_density(aes(ra1cw0), fill = bu_lightgreen, alpha = .3) +
  geom_density(aes(ra0cw1), fill = bu_palegreen,  alpha = .3) +
  geom_density(aes(ra1cw1), fill = bu_grey,       alpha = .4) +
  annotate("text", x = 5.7,  y = .55, label = "open access,\nno civil war",   color = bu_black, size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = 13.6, y = .45, label = "open access,\ncivil war",      color = bu_black, size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = 16.8, y = .35, label = "restricted access,\nno civil war", color = bu_green, size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = 24.7, y = .30, label = "restricted access,\ncivil war",    color = bu_black, size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Simulated expected scarring for four scenarios",
       x = "Expected scarring torture", y = "density") +
  theme_minimal()









Four clearly separated distributions. Restricted access shifts the whole distribution right by about eleven allegations; civil war by about eight; together they stack. And because we have the full simulated distribution, not just a point, we can read directly the probability that, say, a restricted-access country in civil war has higher expected scarring than an open one at peace — the overlap between two of these densities. That is the flexibility King, Tomz, and Wittenberg were after, and it is why simulation is the default when the quantity gets complicated.

title: Exercise #1 — Distributions, Simulation, and the Log-Likelihood
text:
Notes
The CES project site is https://cces.gov.harvard.edu. Here’s an article about the “American Voter Bot” project: https://www.nytimes.com/2020/01/20/opinion/twitter-democratic-debate.html

title: Likelihood Theory & Estimation Mechanics
text:
Last week we built a model for a binary \(y\) from the ground up. We looked at \(y\), wrote down the probability distribution that described it, took the joint probability of the whole sample, logged it, made the distribution’s parameter a function of \(x\beta\), and chose a link function \(F\) to map the linear prediction on the appropriate (probability) space. Six steps, and at the end of them we were holding a log-likelihood function:
\[
\ell(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[\, y_i \log \pi_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-\pi_i)\,\big],
\qquad \pi_i = F(x_i\beta).
\]
Then we used glm to estimate the logit and generated quantities of interest.
What we haven’t covered is how the model got estimated — what goes on in the magic box when we call glm with a binomial family and a logit link. Filling that gap is the task here, answering these questions:

What is a likelihood, and how does it differ from a probability?
Given data and a log-likelihood, how do we solve for the unknowns — and what, dimensionally, are we solving?
Why are some estimates precise with small standard errors and others are not, and how does that arise from the data and the math of likelihood?

This will illustrate something we mentioned last week. In interpretation, a nonlinear model differs from a linear one in exactly one respect: we transform the linear prediction by \(F\). In estimation, the two technologies are genuinely different. OLS gives you a single formula to apply to the data. Maximum likelihood, in almost every case we care about, does not — it builds a formula out of the data, then tries different “models,” comparing them until it finds the one most likely to have generated what we observed.

title: Likelihood Theory & Estimation Mechanics
text:
The binomial log-likelihood, written out
Make it concrete with the binomial, the model from last week. For a single binary outcome \(y_i\), write \(\pi_i = Pr(y_i = 1)\) for the probability of a one. The density of one observation is the Bernoulli, and we map the linear predictor \(x_i\beta\) into that probability with a link function \(F\):
\[
f(y_i \mid \pi_i) = \pi_i^{y_i}(1-\pi_i)^{1-y_i},
\qquad
\pi_i = F(x_i\beta).
\]
Take the log of that density, sum over the \(n\) observations, and substitute the link for \(\pi_i\). That gives us the form we will use for the rest of the semester:
\[
\ell(\beta) \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[\;
\underbrace{y_i \log F(x_i\beta)}_{\text{the ones}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{(1-y_i)\log\big(1 - F(x_i\beta)\big)}_{\text{the zeros}}
\;\Big]
\]
Read it as two mirror-image parts, because that’s what it is. The \(y_i\) out front of the first term and the \((1-y_i)\) out front of the second are doing switching work: when \(y_i = 1\) the second term is multiplied by zero and vanishes, and when \(y_i = 0\) the first term vanishes. So every observation in the sample contributes exactly one of the two, never both. The ones contribute \(\log Pr(y_i = 1)\), and the zeros contribute \(\log Pr(y_i = 0)\).
That reading tells you what maximizing this thing actually does. We are looking for the \(\beta\) that simultaneously pushes \(F(x_i\beta)\) up toward one at every row where we observed a dispute, and pushes it down toward zero at every row where we didn’t. Those two demands pull in opposite directions — the same coefficient has to serve both — and \(\widehat\beta\) is the best available compromise between them. When we say maximum likelihood “makes the observed data as probable as possible,” this is the arithmetic of that sentence.
Now notice where the link sits. \(F\) appears in both halves and nowhere else. Everything that distinguishes one binary model from another lives inside those two \(F\)’s, which is why swapping the link is the whole difference between a logit and a probit. Written out:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{logit:}\quad
\ell(\beta) &= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[\, y_i \log \Lambda(x_i\beta) + (1-y_i)\log\big(1-\Lambda(x_i\beta)\big)\,\Big],
&& \Lambda(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}} \\[6pt]
\text{probit:}\quad
\ell(\beta) &= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[\, y_i \log \Phi(x_i\beta) + (1-y_i)\log\big(1-\Phi(x_i\beta)\big)\,\Big],
&& \Phi(z) = \int_{-\infty}^{z}\phi(u)\,du
\end{aligned}
\]
Same structure, same two parts, one substitution. Hold onto that; when we get to counts and durations we will write down log-likelihoods that look nothing like these, and the thing that stays constant is the procedure, not the formula.






An aside: the logit’s compact form, and why the coefficients are log-odds



For the logit specifically — and only the logit — the two parts can be regrouped into something more compact. Distribute the \((1-y_i)\), gather the two \(y_i\) terms into a single log of a ratio, and that ratio \(\pi_i/(1-\pi_i)\) is the odds that \(y_i = 1\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell(\beta)
&= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[\, y_i \log \pi_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-\pi_i)\,\big] \\[4pt]
&= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[\, y_i \log \pi_i - y_i \log(1-\pi_i) + \log(1-\pi_i)\,\big] \\[4pt]
&= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[\, y_i \log\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i} + \log(1-\pi_i)\,\Big] \\[4pt]
&= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[\, y_i\, x_i\beta - \log\!\big(1 + e^{x_i\beta}\big)\,\big].
\end{aligned}
\]
The last step is where the logit earns its keep: the logit link sets the log-odds equal to the linear predictor, \(\log[\pi_i/(1-\pi_i)] = x_i\beta\), exactly — which is the fact behind the odds-ratio interpretation we used last week. And since \(\pi_i = 1/(1+e^{-x_i\beta})\), rearranging gives \(1-\pi_i = 1/(1+e^{x_i\beta})\), so \(\log(1-\pi_i) = -\log(1+e^{x_i\beta})\).
It’s worth seeing once, because you will meet it in textbooks and because it explains the log-odds scale. But don’t take it as the general form — it is a logit-only convenience. The probit has no such regrouping; \(\Phi\) doesn’t oblige. The two-part version above is the one that generalizes, so that’s the one we’ll write.

title: Likelihood Theory & Estimation Mechanics
text:
Where the algebra works
Take the binomial with no \(x\) variables at all. Every observation shares the same probability \(\pi\) — there is one unknown, a single number, and we want the value of it that makes our observed string of zeros and ones most probable. Write the log-likelihood, differentiate with respect to \(\pi\), set it to zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell(\pi) &= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[\, y_i\log\pi + (1-y_i)\log(1-\pi)\,\big] \\[4pt]
          &= \Big(\textstyle\sum_i y_i\Big)\log\pi \;+\; \Big(n - \textstyle\sum_i y_i\Big)\log(1-\pi) \\[4pt]
\frac{d\ell}{d\pi} &= \frac{\sum_i y_i}{\pi} \;-\; \frac{n - \sum_i y_i}{1-\pi} \;=\; 0 \\[4pt]
(1-\pi)\textstyle\sum_i y_i &= \pi\Big(n - \textstyle\sum_i y_i\Big) \\[4pt]
\textstyle\sum_i y_i &= \pi\, n \\[4pt]
\widehat\pi &= \bbox[#A7DA92, 3pt, border: 1px solid #005A43]{\;\frac{\sum_i y_i}{n} \;=\; \bar y\;}
\end{aligned}
\]
The second line just counts: \(\sum_i y_i\) observations contribute a \(\log\pi\), the remaining \(n - \sum_i y_i\) contribute a \(\log(1-\pi)\). Two steps of algebra from there, and the answer is the sample mean of \(y\). No software, no starting value, no algorithm — a formula.
On the dispute data, that formula says the maximum likelihood estimate of \(\pi\) is the observed dispute rate:


code
dp <- read_dta(here::here("data", "dp.dta"))
dp$lncaprat <- log(dp$caprat)   # a capability ratio is multiplicative, so model it on the log scale

round(mean(dp$dispute), 4)


[1] 0.0451


Now the same thing with a different distribution, to show this isn’t a peculiarity of the binomial. Suppose \(y\) is a count — Snickers bars without peanuts produced in an 8 hour shift — so the Poisson, whose parameter \(\lambda\) is the rate at which events occur. Density, log-likelihood, derivative:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(y_i \mid \lambda) &= \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{y_i}}{y_i!} \\[4pt]
\ell(\lambda) &= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[\, -\lambda + y_i\log\lambda - \log(y_i!)\,\big] \\[4pt]
              &= -n\lambda \;+\; \Big(\textstyle\sum_i y_i\Big)\log\lambda \;-\; \textstyle\sum_i \log(y_i!) \\[4pt]
\frac{d\ell}{d\lambda} &= -n + \frac{\sum_i y_i}{\lambda} \;=\; 0 \\[4pt]
\widehat\lambda &= \bbox[#A7DA92, 3pt, border: 1px solid #005A43]{\;\frac{\sum_i y_i}{n} \;=\; \bar y\;}
\end{aligned}
\]
Again a formula, again the sample mean. Note the \(\log(y_i!)\) term: no \(\lambda\) in it, so it vanishes on differentiation. It is part of the likelihood’s magnitude, and magnitude carries no information.
Try it on a small set of real counts. Here are Snickers bars without peanuts produced in an 8 hour shift, one count per shift:
\[
y = \{5,\; 0,\; 1,\; 1,\; 0,\; 3,\; 2,\; 3,\; 4,\; 1\}
\]
That first shift doesn’t like peanuts.


code
cw <- c(5, 0, 1, 1, 0, 3, 2, 3, 4, 1)

c(sum_y      = sum(cw),
  n          = length(cw),
  lambda_hat = sum(cw) / length(cw),
  glm_check  = unname(exp(coef(glm(cw ~ 1, family = poisson)))))


     sum_y          n lambda_hat  glm_check 
        20         10          2          2 


\(\widehat\lambda = 20/10 = 2\), and a Poisson glm with nothing but a constant agrees exactly.
So: two different distributions, two different parameters, the same procedure — write \(\ell\), differentiate, set to zero, solve — and a closed-form answer both times.2 Figure 3 draws both log-likelihoods, with the closed-form answer marked on each.


code
# Two distributions, two parameters, the same shape of problem. Each curve is
# the log-likelihood over its one unknown; each dashed line is the value the
# algebra produced. I plot RELATIVE log-likelihood (subtracting the maximum) so
# the two panels are comparable -- remember the level carries no information.

pi_hat  <- mean(dp$dispute)
g_pi    <- seq(0.030, 0.070, length.out = 400)
ll_pi   <- sum(dp$dispute) * log(g_pi) + sum(1 - dp$dispute) * log(1 - g_pi)

p_bern <- ggplot(tibble(pi = g_pi, rel = ll_pi - max(ll_pi)), aes(pi, rel)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = bu_green) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = pi_hat, linetype = "dashed", color = bu_black) +
