What the deck became over 2026-09-03 to 09-05 (D23 and its amendments): average-effects plot with bands; the Uncertainty section worked with examples (delta vs EPT on full data and on a 500-case refit; a quadratic model for the linear-combination SE; bootstrap vs KTW at one profile with a four-technique table); “Average effects, two ways” rebuilt as explicit loops with tidy versions in comments; “When the two techniques disagree”; “Which to choose, and when” replacing the Take-away; all 14 figures numbered and cross-referenced. Dave did a language pass through ~line 120 and the rest was swept to match (“these slides,” no coined labels).
T10 done. The three llfmax26.qmd chunks hidden for exercise #2 are visible again and the re-rendered deck is staged.
The substantive thing to remember about the CES data: two of the seven policy items run backwards from their names. aca == "Support" means support repealing the ACA, and mandmin == "Support" means support eliminating mandatory minimums. Both are silent — the recode runs, glm converges, the sign is just wrong. The codebook says so; the answer key doesn’t use either variable.
Open: T11 (Ex #3 contradicts Ex #2), T12 (starting values), T4, D14’s citation loose end. T13 (voice pass on prediction26) is effectively done — Dave read and edited.




D1 — Prune the search index rather than drop it. docs/search.json stays tracked, but prune-search-index.sh trims it to published pages before each commit. Rationale: dropping it kills site search entirely, which gets more useful as decks are released weekly. The alternative — render unreleased decks to a separate output dir — would fight the deliberate no-render:-list design in _quarto.yml (a full-render prune would delete the local reference copies in docs/).
D2 — The pruner derives its allowlist from .gitignore. It reads the !docs/<page>.html un-ignore lines rather than keeping a second list. Rationale: releasing a deck stays a one-place edit, matching the release recipe already written into .gitignore’s header comment. A new deck released without re-running the pruner simply won’t be searchable — it fails closed, never open.
D3 — This worklog is untracked. Added to .gitignore. Rationale: it names unreleased decks and answer keys; the repo is public.
D4 — Rewrite history rather than only fixing forward. git filter-branch --index-filter stripped docs/search.json from all 8 commits. Rationale: GitHub’s file-history UI makes prior blobs a two-click read, and the leaked content includes exercise answer keys. Cost is zero — the repo is public but has 0 forks, 0 stars, and no collaborators. Backup bundle of the pre-rewrite history: MLEfall26-pre-rewrite.bundle, pre-rewrite main = 01ccaa70. Local refs/original/* were deleted.
D5 — Ignore the htmlwidgets/plotly site_libs. Extended the existing byproduct block to crosstalk*, htmltools-fill*, htmlwidgets*, jquery*, plotly-*, typedarray*. Verified none of the seven published pages reference them (decks use embed-resources: true).
D6 — Track and link binarymodels26.R. The deck was released but its companion script was untracked and unlinked, unlike predictionOLS26.R. Added to the repo and to code.qmd, noting that dp.dta comes through Brightspace (only ITT.csv is published).
D7 — gh as the git credential path. The terminal could not push: GitHub dropped password auth over HTTPS, this machine has no SSH keys, and the osxkeychain helper was empty. Pushes had been going through GitHub Desktop, which keeps its own credential store. Installed gh (Homebrew, 2.97.0), Dave ran gh auth login --web, then gh auth setup-git wired credential.https://github.com.helper. Rationale: browser OAuth, no token to store or rotate, and it fixes pushes for all seven repos on this machine. Rejected pushing from GitHub Desktop — after a history rewrite it offers to pull first, and a merge would have spliced the leaked blobs back in.
Amended 2026-08-19 (session 7): that rejection was specific to the rewrite, not standing. GitHub Desktop is fine for ordinary commits. The test is divergence: if git rev-list --left-right --count main...origin/main is 0 0 (or you are only ahead), Desktop has nothing to merge and pushing from it is identical to pushing from the terminal. Avoid Desktop only when local history has been rewritten and origin still holds the old commits.
D8 — The pruner stays manual; no pre-commit hook. Dave’s call, 2026-08-19. Rationale: git hooks aren’t tracked, so a hook would vanish on a fresh clone or a new machine and leave a safety net that silently isn’t there — worse than a step you know you have to take. Step 3 of the release workflow below is the guard. Revisit only if the leak recurs.
D9 — Exercise #1 Part II stays a LOGIT. Do not switch it to the cloglog. It was switched to cloglog on 2026-08-19 and reverted the same day; this entry exists so it does not get switched a third time. The cloglog is attractive here — it makes Part II internally consistent with question 2 and pays that figure off immediately. It is wrong anyway, because of what it does to Exercise #2: Ex#2 Q2 (“A log-likelihood you were not handed”) asks students to write the cloglog log-likelihood in math and in R, and Ex#2 Q2 also asks them to compare it to the logit log-likelihood, which Ex#1 Q6 is the only place that assigns. Putting the cloglog in Ex#1 both spoils Ex#2’s central exercise and removes the baseline it is measured against. Logit in Ex#1, cloglog in Ex#2, and the two links stay a week apart. Q7 evaluates at the glm logit estimates accordingly. Verified values in the key: truth −526.602, glm logit −526.500, all zeros −693.147, sign-flipped −1273.240; glm returns (−0.996, 0.518, −0.463).
D10 — Answer-key figures must be byte-identical to the exercise’s replication targets. The key’s figures 2–4 had carried subtitle= lines the exercise’s did not. Students are told to replicate exactly, so a key that shows a different figure is a trap. Subtitles stripped from the key; the claims they made already appear in the key’s prose. Verified by md5 across all four figures. Standing rule for every future exercise/key pair.
D12 — Exercises live on the renamed code.qmd, not a new page. Dave’s call, 2026-08-19. The page title became “Exercises & Code” (the navbar entry is bare, so it inherits the title — no text: override, and the nav label and page heading agree); the filename and the code.html URL are unchanged. Sections: Exercises, Code, Data. Rationale: code.qmd is already released and already in the pruner’s allowlist, so this adds zero new publishing surface — a new exercises.qmd would have needed !exercises.qmd, !docs/exercises.html, a navbar entry, and a pruner allowlist entry, which is four more chances to get a release wrong in a repo that has already leaked once. Cost: by week 10 the page carries five exercises plus ten decks; toc: true gives it anchors, and splitting later is cheap. Deleted the commented block that had linked “exercise #1” and “exercise #2” to the answer keys — Pandoc passed it through, so docs/code.html had been naming both key files on the live site.
D13 — Releasing an exercise publishes the HTML only; the .qmd is never un-ignored. The exercise .qmd is not merely “source” — its echo=FALSE figure chunks are the complete answers to questions 1–4. Released deck sources (predictionOLS26.qmd, binarymodels26.qmd) stay published on purpose, so students have a template for YAML, chunk options, LaTeX, and the ggplot idiom; exercise sources never are. Verified 2026-08-19 that the released decks don’t spoil Part I: binarymodels26.qmd plots logit/probit CDFs with plogis/pnorm/dlogis (which Part I forbids) and contains no Cauchy, cloglog, loglog, intercept-shift, or scobit code. Verified the published page carries no source: docs/ex12026.html has zero <pre> blocks, zero hits for normal_pdf, atan(z), pivot_longer, geom_line, exp(-exp(z)), series_colors, or set.seed, four base64 figures, and no external references. Its only <code> spans are backticked words from the prose. And git add -A --dry-run does not list ex12026.qmd — an ignored file cannot enter a commit, so no push can carry it.
D15 — Nothing public names Claude, and no public file explains the hold-out scheme. Dave’s call, 2026-08-20. Two separate tells, both fixed.
The “collaborator.” Claude was never a GitHub collaborator — clavedark was and is the only one, and the only contributor. What Dave saw was commit a5fb2d6, which carried a Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 trailer; GitHub renders such a commit with two avatars, which reads as a second person on the repo. Removing a trailer means rewriting the commit, so git filter-branch --msg-filter over a5fb2d6~1..HEAD stripped it and, in the same pass, reworded that commit’s subject. Do not add Co-Authored-By trailers to commits in this repo.
The commit message. GitHub’s file table shows the last commit message beside each file, and a5fb2d6’s subject — “Stop the search index from leaking unreleased material” — was sitting next to both binarymodels26.R and prune-search-index.sh, announcing to any student that unreleased material exists and that there was a leak worth hunting. Reworded to “Add search index pruning; track binarymodels26.R”.
The file comments. prune-search-index.sh’s header said it holds “decks, exercise answer keys, and side projects” out of the public repo; .gitignore’s comments spelled out the entire scheme, said the search index “leaks unreleased decks and answer keys,” and noted that answer keys stay out “regardless.” All trimmed to operational notes — the release recipe future-Dave needs, none of the rationale. Standing rule: tracked files carry operational notes only; the reasoning lives in this worklog, which is untracked. Verified every non-comment line of .gitignore byte-identical before and after, and that ex12026.qmd, ex12026answers.qmd, clarkreed.dta, and worklog.md are still ignored while ces.csv and binarymodels26.qmd are still published.
Rewrite mechanics, for next time: backup bundle at scratchpad/MLEfall26-pre-msg-rewrite.bundle (pre-rewrite main = d07c14c); refs/original/* deleted, reflog expired, git gc --prune=now; verified git diff origin/main HEAD~1 empty, i.e. only messages changed; pushed with --force-with-lease pinned to the old SHA. Post-push checks: 0 non-clavedark commits, 0 commits matching claude/anthropic, collaborators = clavedark only.
D14 — ces.csv is published in the repo; the exercise links it directly. Dave’s call, 2026-08-19, after being offered a gzipped version and a Brightspace-only fallback. The exercise said “Here’s a link to a dataset called ces.csv” and there was no link and no published file. Now !data/ces.csv in .gitignore, linked from exercise #1 and from the Data section of the Exercises & Code page, with data/README.md rewritten around two exceptions rather than one.
Amended 2026-08-19 (session 8b): the exercise links to the Data section, not to GitHub. The first version anchored the link on the ces.csv code span, pointing straight at the GitHub blob URL, and Dave read the sentence as having no link at all. It now reads [Here's a link](code.qmd#data) — plain words as the anchor, landing on the Data section of the Exercises & Code page, which is where the download link and the source credit already live. One place to maintain, and the GitHub-specific “click Download raw file” note stays on the code page instead of being repeated in the exercise. General lesson: don’t anchor a link on an inline code span when the sentence announces a link. Rationale: zero friction — students click one link, and the key’s read_csv(here::here("data", "ces.csv")) needs no change. Rejected the 1.0 MB gzip (13× smaller, and read_csv() reads .gz transparently — verified, 61,000 × 20) because Safari auto-gunzips .gz downloads, so some students would end up with a filename that doesn’t match the path in the code; that is a week-one support ticket for a saving nobody sees. Cost accepted: 13 MB, the largest tracked file in the repo, permanent in history (tracked payload 30 MB → 43 MB). The published page tells students GitHub won’t preview a file that size and to click Download raw file. Loose end: the source credit is the CES project site, not a formal citation — the ITT entry has a full one and this should match. Not written here because the exact Dataverse citation was not verified.
D11 — The key answers the question asked, quotes the question, and stops. Dave’s call, 2026-08-19, after two rounds of trimming. Three rules, all of which the key had been violating:

Every answer opens with its question, verbatim, as a blockquote. Students read the key days or weeks after doing the work, and a heading like “CDFs and PDFs” does not tell them what was asked. All ten questions plus the Part I and Part III preambles are quoted.
Answer the question and nothing adjacent. Question 1 asks what the PDFs and CDFs describe; the key had also explained why the CDF rather than the PDF is the link and how the three distributions differ in the tails. Both cut — the second is question 2’s job anyway. Question 6 says “describe the parts,” and the parts are the \(y=1\) term and the \(y=0\) term; that answer is now about those two and why the two-part form is written instead of the log-odds form, with the product-and-logs material demoted to one paragraph and the log-odds display gone.
No enrichment sections. The simulated-median panel, the two-panel comparison figure, and the delta-versus-simulation table were removed outright, not relabeled. A “Beyond the assignment” heading was the previous attempt and it was the wrong fix: length itself is the problem, because a key long enough to skim is a key nobody learns from afterwards. Same reasoning removed the se.fit-shortcut digression from question 10. Simulation-based intervals belong in a deck, not in an exercise key. Net: 957 → 882 lines with the question text added back in.

Also under this: the probit at-means chunk ended in a bare all.equal(...) that printed a stray TRUE into the prose. Now stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(...))) — silent on success, stops the render on failure, and a better habit to model.
D16 — The CES codebook is descriptions only, published complete. Dave’s call, 2026-08-24, in two steps. First: publish it, and tell students everything — “provide all the info they need… I’m interested in informing them completely.” That closed T7 against holding the item directions back to preserve the reverse-engineering work in question 8. Second, and the more consequential edit: no descriptive statistics. The first draft carried a frequency table for every categorical, summary statistics and a histogram for age, a missingness table, an empirical direction-evidence table, and a recode recipe. All of it went. “I really just want variable descriptions and nothing else — include only essential notes like which direction a variable runs.”
Rationale, and it is worth holding onto because it will come up again: a codebook answers what is this variable, and every distribution printed in it is a number the student should be generating themselves. Printing the frequencies doesn’t inform them, it does their count() calls for them — and it buries the one thing they can’t derive, which is what “Support” means on aca. The finished page is four tables of name/description/values/notes and about a page of prose. The supporting analysis that established the directions is not in it; it lives in this log and in the scratch profile, and the page says only that the directions were established from the data with aca as the worked example.

D22 — The build template is a hand-rolled Newton-Raphson, mirroring Exercise #2 (2026-08-30, Dave’s call). optim is no longer the estimator; it is a check run at the end. The file is now 13 steps built on three functions and a loop, with Exercise #2’s signatures and argument order (beta, X, y), its fit_*(X, y, tol = 1e-8, maxit = 50) shape, and its return list (coef, se, vcov, loglik, iterations, converged, history). Names are neutral — mle_ll, mle_score, mle_hessian, fit_mle — because pois_ll would answer Step 1.
Three things that had to be worked out rather than assumed:

The \(\beta = \mathbf{0}\) test is cleaner here than in the logit. Ex #2 sets every coefficient to zero so \(\pi_i = 0.5\) and the weight is \(0.25\). Under the exp link the same move gives \(\lambda_i = 1\) for everybody, so \(\ell(\mathbf{0}) = -n - \sum\ln(y_i!)\), \(s(\mathbf{0}) = X'(y - \mathbf{1})\), and \(H(\mathbf{0}) = -X'X\) — no constant to carry at all. Each piece gets its own pass/fail row before the estimator runs.
Starting values matter more than they look. From \(\beta = \mathbf{0}\) NR takes 26 iterations on these data and the first step overshoots the intercept badly enough to drive the log-likelihood to \(-3.4\times10^{11}\) before it crawls back. From \(\beta_0 = (\ln\bar y, 0, \ldots)\) it takes 6, monotone throughout. The key uses the latter and says why; the student file tells them a better intercept guess exists without naming it.
The monotone-log-likelihood check needs a tolerance, and finding that out was worth it. The increments are \(325\), \(14.5\), \(0.052\), \(1.1\mathrm{e}{-6}\), \(-2.7\mathrm{e}{-12}\) — the last one negative, because at the top the log-likelihood stops changing at machine precision. A strict all(diff(loglik) > 0) printed FALSE on a fit that matches glm to ten decimals. Now > -1e-6, and the key explains the arithmetic rather than hiding it.

The intercept-only warm-up was dropped: with \(\ln\bar y\) starting values it converges in one iteration by construction, so it stopped being a test. The \(\beta = \mathbf{0}\) tests do that job better. optim moved to Step 10, where negating \(\ell\) and \(s\) is a minus sign rather than a new derivation, and where dropping gr shows the 0.0022 intercept gap that a numerical derivative costs.

T12 — Reconsider the starting values in the binary materials (opened 2026-08-31; do not touch before 2026-09-02). Dave: “why don’t we do this in the binomial models, ie start with mean y plus k-1 zeros for starting values instead of all zeros?” Tested rather than argued. On the course dispute logit (dispute ~ lncaprat + border + deml, n = 20,990) Newton-Raphson takes 8 iterations from \(\mathbf{0}\) and 6 from \((\mathrm{logit}(\bar y), 0, \ldots)\) — same estimates, monotone either way. So it helps, but it is not a repair.
The mechanism, which is the part worth teaching. It is not distance: \(\beta = \mathbf{0}\) is further from the intercept-only solution in link space for the logit (\(|\mathrm{logit}(.045)| =
3.05\)) than for the Poisson (\(|\ln 8.13| = 2.10\)). It is the weight Newton divides by. Logit weight at \(\mathbf{0}\) is \(\pi(1-\pi) = 0.25\) against \(0.042\) at the solution — 6x too steep, so the step comes out too short; and \(0.25\) is the maximum \(\pi(1-\pi)\) can take, so \(\beta = \mathbf{0}\) is the most conservative start a logit has. Poisson weight at \(\mathbf{0}\) is \(\lambda = 1\) against \(8.13\) — 8x too flat, so the step overshoots.
Verified the falsifiable implication rather than stopping at the story: simulated Poissons sweeping \(\bar y\) = 0.25, 0.64, 1.15, 1.88, 5.2, 9.2, 23.2 take 7, 6, 6, 7, 13, 23, 58 iterations from \(\mathbf{0}\) and 5 from \(\ln\bar y\) every time. Below \(\bar y \approx 1\) zeros are fine; above it the cost grows without bound (first-iteration log-likelihood \(-1.9\times10^{26}\) at \(\bar y = 23\)). The bounded inverse link is what protects the logit.

The note, answered. Rewrote it around the two-step lookup: R looks inside the function first (arguments, plus anything the body made), then in your workspace. So the fix is simply to make it an argument — the local binding always wins, and the leak only happens for names you forgot to declare. Then the part that was missing, how to prove there is no leak: rename the outside objects so the names disagree (design/outcome, rm(X, y)) and call the function again. Dave’s note. “Why does 6 indicate there’s a bug, but 2 doesn’t? Would 4? What’s the threshold here? Why?” A fair hit: the passage asserted 2-versus-6 without justifying the cut.
Computed it rather than hand-waving. The relevant probability is not \(P(\lvert z\rvert > c)\) for one coefficient but \(P(\text{any of } k > c) = 1-(1-p)^k\), because you look at all \(k\) and react to the largest. Addendum 5 — the Hessian’s lambda * X line needed a dimension walk. Dave: “this looks like a kxn matrix times (lxn *nxk) … how do the dimensions sort out here?” The reading that trips people is treating * as matrix multiplication. Row \(i\) is scaled by \(\lambda_i\), the result is still \(n \times k\), and t(X) %*% it is \((k \times n)(n \times k) = k
\times k\). Verified against diag(lambda) %*% X and against an explicit \(\sum_i \lambda_i x_i'x_i\) loop on a 3-by-2 toy; all three agree.

Software claims verified (Dave asked). marginaleffects 0.20.1 inferences(method = "simulation") draws R coefficient vectors from MVN(coef, vcov), computes the estimand per draw, takes quantiles — the help page cites Krinsky & Robb (1986) and King, Tomz & Wittenberg (2000). It also offers method = "boot" / "fwb" / "rsample" (resample the data, refit). Clarify (Tomz, Wittenberg & King 2003, JSS 8(1), Stata) and Zelig implement KTW; Zelig additionally had bootstrap = TRUE/n (nonparametric: resample + rerun) and its docs call the normal sim() algorithm “a form of the parametric bootstrap.” The R clarify package (Greifer, Worthington, Iacus & King, R Journal 2025) is the Zelig successor, KTW only. Deck sentence amended accordingly. Bootstrapping QIs in polisci: Hanmer & Kalkan 2013 fn. lists “delta method, bootstrapping, or simulation (see Herron 1999; King, Tomz, and Wittenberg 2000)” and use simulation themselves; Mooney 1996 AJPS 40:570-602 is the discipline’s bootstrap piece (seats/votes example); Carsey & Harden 2014 (Sage) is the textbook. Herron 1999 (PA 8:83-98) discusses a parametric bootstrap for predicted probabilities, which is the KTW draw under another name — full text not reached, so that characterization is from secondary sources.
2026-09-04 — “Average effects, two ways” rebuilt (Dave). He flagged the opener (“This is the mixing made concrete…”) as impenetrable and asked that the section rebuild the average effect before attaching delta and simulation, plus say briefly when the two would not overlap. Now: an ae-rebuild chunk defines cf_X(d) (counterfactual design matrix) and recomputes the average effect from X %*% b, printing the max difference from the predict() loop; ae-delta and ae-sim both call cf_X() and read as “the rebuild plus two lines.” New ### When the two techniques disagree uses the existing m_small (n = 500) refit: delta band crosses zero from Polity 0 on, simulated band lopsided and positive (checked: at Polity 10 delta [-0.0019, 0.0033] vs sim [0.00002, 0.027]; at full n the two agree everywhere, sim upper/lower ratio ~1.15).
ae-rebuild check dropped (Dave). The max(abs(...)) line printed an orphaned 0; Dave declined a comparison table too. The chunk now just recomputes the average effect, and one sentence says it is the same quantity as Figure 3, recomputed so the code sits with the delta and simulation chunks.
Bootstrap chunk: replicate() version added as a commented “MORE EFFICIENT” block (Dave). The prose note about replicate(B, { ... }) stays; students can now see the code.
Then scaled back (Dave: “too much — my fault”). fig-case-dist is back to two markers (mean solid green, at-means dashed black); median/mode lines were hard to tell apart. Prose cut to: what the density is, mean = average effect, at-means to its right and why, distribution slides left with democracy, one sentence on narrowing (steep vs flat part of the curve). The odds-ratio / “interaction in differences but not ratios” discussion is gone — no big point students need. The numbers stay in the entry below for reference.
2026-09-05, later still — figures numbered; case-distribution figure rebuilt (Dave). All 14 figure chunks now carry #| label: fig-* + #| fig-cap: (chunk headers made bare {r} so the old duplicate-label warning on fig-max-me is gone); prose references converted to @fig-*. fig-case-dist now marks mean, median, mode, and at-means with a linetype legend, and the prose says plainly that each panel is the density of the n individual predictions from which the average is taken. Numbers behind the prose (border = 0): mean/median/mode = .0393/.0350/.0313 at Polity -10, .0200/.0177/.0157 at 0, .0100/.0088/.0078 at 10 — right-skewed, mean > median > mode in each. SD of predictions .0189/.0099/.0050 while SD of x’b is 0.512 in every panel (democracy is a constant shift on the link scale); 95th/5th percentile ratio 5.2/5.3/5.4. The lesson written: compression is the link, absolute spread shrinks, relative spread does not — a logit with no interaction term implies interaction in differences but not in odds ratios.
2026-09-05, later — Dave’s language pass through ~line 120, then a sweep (Dave). His edits: “this file” → “these slides”; “we point back to” → “we’ll refer back to”; “read them off” → “examined”; “the two crossed” → “joined together to form the confidence interval”. Register: plainer and a shade softer. Swept the rest: seven remaining “this file / the file” → “these slides”; “pile” (5x) → set/distribution; dropped “earns its keep,” “the one guessing,” “not a thing,” “Now the payoff,” “honest resampling,” “hands back,” “That is the whole technique.” Note for future drafting in this deck: Dave calls the decks “slides” and the other decks “notes” (“binary response notes”).
2026-09-05 — “# Which to choose, and when” added (Dave). Replaces the Take-away. Three subsections plus a six-item short version: at-means vs average effects (Dave’s argument — at-means easier to write but single-case and possibly a case that does not exist; especially bad with fixed effects, where the FE must be held at the reference unit or a nonexistent mean; average effects let the data speak in the real cases and keep each case’s FE); analytic vs simulated (same asymptotic foundation; analytic is deterministic and what the software returns; simulate for nonlinear multi-parameter QIs, small n, boundaries; bootstrap when N(b, V) itself is in doubt); ML vs delta (ML + EPT for a monotone transform of one linear prediction; delta when there is no single link scale: averages, marginal effects, first differences, multinomial). Also: Dave reported still seeing “first-pass band” and no “disagree” subsection — the source and docs/prediction26.html both had the fixes; he was reading the Sep 3 HTML sent via SendUserFile or a cached tab. Fresh file sent. The ae-small chunk converted to a loop to match the section.
2026-09-05 — loops, not map_dfr, in “Average effects, two ways” (Dave: “my interest is in showing the process”). The rebuild, delta, and simulation chunks are now explicit loops with preallocated vectors and the design matrix set inline (Xi <- X; Xi[, "deml"] <- ...); the cf_X() + map_dfr versions are kept as commented “MORE EFFICIENT” blocks, the OLS deck’s pattern. The delta prose is broken into one equation per line — the average, the general delta form, the one-case derivative via the chain rule, the gradient as the average of those, the SE — and a paragraph walks the three new code lines (w, colMeans(w * Xi), the quadratic form). Dave asked for the delta chunk only; I did all three in the section for consistency (reversible).
“first-pass band” struck (Dave: “sounds like a bad boy band from the 90s”). All six uses replaced with plain description (“the averaged case-level intervals”). Standing rule, now in memory: don’t coin a name for a device; describe it.
Ribbons darkened (Dave). Every filled geom_ribbon in the deck is now alpha = 0.5 (was .2-.3); the dotted-outline ribbon in ae-compare (fill = NA) untouched.
Open. T13 (voice pass; also release mechanics). T10 is now past its date.
Next. Dave reads the rendered docs/prediction26.html, marks drift; then decide on release (.gitignore un-ignore + code.qmd link + prune + push).



Done. Loops in “Average effects, two ways” with tidy versions commented; delta prose one equation per line; replicate() version of the bootstrap in comments; figures numbered (14) with @fig- references; Figure 5 (individual predictions behind the average) redrawn, then scaled back at Dave’s request to mean + at-means only; the ae-rebuild check dropped; “Which to choose, and when” added; language sweep after Dave’s pass. Released per the deck workflow: un-ignore lines, render of prediction26, predictionOLS26 (forward mention now a link), and slides, pruner run, files staged. Dave commits and pushes.
Also staged, same session: the exercise #2 answer key (docs/ex22026answers.html, code.qmd link, .gitignore, pruned index). With the key public, hiding the three llfmax26 chunks protects nothing — T10 is the obvious companion and was not done here.
And T10 done: the three llfmax26 chunks (dev2-step, nr, fig-starts) restored to echo: true, the header note about hiding them removed, deck re-rendered and pruned, staged.
Next. Commit/push. Then T11 (Ex #3 contradicts Ex #2).

title: MLEfall26 — worklog
text:
Two releases staged; Dave commits and pushes. (1) prediction26 (below). (2) The exercise #2 answer key, same recipe as the ex #1 key (session 21): only docs/ex22026answers.html un-ignored, the .qmd stays ignored, linked under the exercise in code.qmd, re-rendered, pruned. The .gitignore comments that said the ex #2 key is “NOT released” / “ignored permanently” are rewritten.
prediction26.qmd is staged for release. Staged: .gitignore (un-ignore lines for the .qmd and the HTML), prediction26.qmd, docs/prediction26.html, slides.qmd + its HTML (new link, last in the list), predictionOLS26.qmd + its HTML (the “once they’re posted” sentence now links to the deck), and the pruned docs/search.json. Not staged, not from this work: binarymodels26.R (modified), likelihood26.R (untracked). No companion .R was made for prediction26; binarymodels26.R is the precedent if one is wanted.
What the deck became over 2026-09-03 to 09-05 (D23 and its amendments): average-effects plot with bands; the Uncertainty section worked with examples (delta vs EPT on full data and on a 500-case refit; a quadratic model for the linear-combination SE; bootstrap vs KTW at one profile with a four-technique table); “Average effects, two ways” rebuilt as explicit loops with tidy versions in comments; “When the two techniques disagree”; “Which to choose, and when” replacing the Take-away; all 14 figures numbered and cross-referenced. Dave did a language pass through ~line 120 and the rest was swept to match (“these slides,” no coined labels).
T10 done. The three llfmax26.qmd chunks hidden for exercise #2 are visible again and the re-rendered deck is staged.
The substantive thing to remember about the CES data: two of the seven policy items run backwards from their names. aca == "Support" means support repealing the ACA, and mandmin == "Support" means support eliminating mandatory minimums. Both are silent — the recode runs, glm converges, the sign is just wrong. The codebook says so; the answer key doesn’t use either variable.
Open: T11 (Ex #3 contradicts Ex #2), T12 (starting values), T4, D14’s citation loose end. T13 (voice pass on prediction26) is effectively done — Dave read and edited.

title: MLEfall26 — worklog
text:
D1 — Prune the search index rather than drop it. docs/search.json stays tracked, but prune-search-index.sh trims it to published pages before each commit. Rationale: dropping it kills site search entirely, which gets more useful as decks are released weekly. The alternative — render unreleased decks to a separate output dir — would fight the deliberate no-render:-list design in _quarto.yml (a full-render prune would delete the local reference copies in docs/).
D2 — The pruner derives its allowlist from .gitignore. It reads the !docs/<page>.html un-ignore lines rather than keeping a second list. Rationale: releasing a deck stays a one-place edit, matching the release recipe already written into .gitignore’s header comment. A new deck released without re-running the pruner simply won’t be searchable — it fails closed, never open.
D3 — This worklog is untracked. Added to .gitignore. Rationale: it names unreleased decks and answer keys; the repo is public.
D4 — Rewrite history rather than only fixing forward. git filter-branch --index-filter stripped docs/search.json from all 8 commits. Rationale: GitHub’s file-history UI makes prior blobs a two-click read, and the leaked content includes exercise answer keys. Cost is zero — the repo is public but has 0 forks, 0 stars, and no collaborators. Backup bundle of the pre-rewrite history: MLEfall26-pre-rewrite.bundle, pre-rewrite main = 01ccaa70. Local refs/original/* were deleted.
D5 — Ignore the htmlwidgets/plotly site_libs. Extended the existing byproduct block to crosstalk*, htmltools-fill*, htmlwidgets*, jquery*, plotly-*, typedarray*. Verified none of the seven published pages reference them (decks use embed-resources: true).
D6 — Track and link binarymodels26.R. The deck was released but its companion script was untracked and unlinked, unlike predictionOLS26.R. Added to the repo and to code.qmd, noting that dp.dta comes through Brightspace (only ITT.csv is published).
D7 — gh as the git credential path. The terminal could not push: GitHub dropped password auth over HTTPS, this machine has no SSH keys, and the osxkeychain helper was empty. Pushes had been going through GitHub Desktop, which keeps its own credential store. Installed gh (Homebrew, 2.97.0), Dave ran gh auth login --web, then gh auth setup-git wired credential.https://github.com.helper. Rationale: browser OAuth, no token to store or rotate, and it fixes pushes for all seven repos on this machine. Rejected pushing from GitHub Desktop — after a history rewrite it offers to pull first, and a merge would have spliced the leaked blobs back in.
Amended 2026-08-19 (session 7): that rejection was specific to the rewrite, not standing. GitHub Desktop is fine for ordinary commits. The test is divergence: if git rev-list --left-right --count main...origin/main is 0 0 (or you are only ahead), Desktop has nothing to merge and pushing from it is identical to pushing from the terminal. Avoid Desktop only when local history has been rewritten and origin still holds the old commits.
D8 — The pruner stays manual; no pre-commit hook. Dave’s call, 2026-08-19. Rationale: git hooks aren’t tracked, so a hook would vanish on a fresh clone or a new machine and leave a safety net that silently isn’t there — worse than a step you know you have to take. Step 3 of the release workflow below is the guard. Revisit only if the leak recurs.
D9 — Exercise #1 Part II stays a LOGIT. Do not switch it to the cloglog. It was switched to cloglog on 2026-08-19 and reverted the same day; this entry exists so it does not get switched a third time. The cloglog is attractive here — it makes Part II internally consistent with question 2 and pays that figure off immediately. It is wrong anyway, because of what it does to Exercise #2: Ex#2 Q2 (“A log-likelihood you were not handed”) asks students to write the cloglog log-likelihood in math and in R, and Ex#2 Q2 also asks them to compare it to the logit log-likelihood, which Ex#1 Q6 is the only place that assigns. Putting the cloglog in Ex#1 both spoils Ex#2’s central exercise and removes the baseline it is measured against. Logit in Ex#1, cloglog in Ex#2, and the two links stay a week apart. Q7 evaluates at the glm logit estimates accordingly. Verified values in the key: truth −526.602, glm logit −526.500, all zeros −693.147, sign-flipped −1273.240; glm returns (−0.996, 0.518, −0.463).
D10 — Answer-key figures must be byte-identical to the exercise’s replication targets. The key’s figures 2–4 had carried subtitle= lines the exercise’s did not. Students are told to replicate exactly, so a key that shows a different figure is a trap. Subtitles stripped from the key; the claims they made already appear in the key’s prose. Verified by md5 across all four figures. Standing rule for every future exercise/key pair.
D12 — Exercises live on the renamed code.qmd, not a new page. Dave’s call, 2026-08-19. The page title became “Exercises & Code” (the navbar entry is bare, so it inherits the title — no text: override, and the nav label and page heading agree); the filename and the code.html URL are unchanged. Sections: Exercises, Code, Data. Rationale: code.qmd is already released and already in the pruner’s allowlist, so this adds zero new publishing surface — a new exercises.qmd would have needed !exercises.qmd, !docs/exercises.html, a navbar entry, and a pruner allowlist entry, which is four more chances to get a release wrong in a repo that has already leaked once. Cost: by week 10 the page carries five exercises plus ten decks; toc: true gives it anchors, and splitting later is cheap. Deleted the commented block that had linked “exercise #1” and “exercise #2” to the answer keys — Pandoc passed it through, so docs/code.html had been naming both key files on the live site.
D13 — Releasing an exercise publishes the HTML only; the .qmd is never un-ignored. The exercise .qmd is not merely “source” — its echo=FALSE figure chunks are the complete answers to questions 1–4. Released deck sources (predictionOLS26.qmd, binarymodels26.qmd) stay published on purpose, so students have a template for YAML, chunk options, LaTeX, and the ggplot idiom; exercise sources never are. Verified 2026-08-19 that the released decks don’t spoil Part I: binarymodels26.qmd plots logit/probit CDFs with plogis/pnorm/dlogis (which Part I forbids) and contains no Cauchy, cloglog, loglog, intercept-shift, or scobit code. Verified the published page carries no source: docs/ex12026.html has zero <pre> blocks, zero hits for normal_pdf, atan(z), pivot_longer, geom_line, exp(-exp(z)), series_colors, or set.seed, four base64 figures, and no external references. Its only <code> spans are backticked words from the prose. And git add -A --dry-run does not list ex12026.qmd — an ignored file cannot enter a commit, so no push can carry it.
D15 — Nothing public names Claude, and no public file explains the hold-out scheme. Dave’s call, 2026-08-20. Two separate tells, both fixed.
The “collaborator.” Claude was never a GitHub collaborator — clavedark was and is the only one, and the only contributor. What Dave saw was commit a5fb2d6, which carried a Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 trailer; GitHub renders such a commit with two avatars, which reads as a second person on the repo. Removing a trailer means rewriting the commit, so git filter-branch --msg-filter over a5fb2d6~1..HEAD stripped it and, in the same pass, reworded that commit’s subject. Do not add Co-Authored-By trailers to commits in this repo.
The commit message. GitHub’s file table shows the last commit message beside each file, and a5fb2d6’s subject — “Stop the search index from leaking unreleased material” — was sitting next to both binarymodels26.R and prune-search-index.sh, announcing to any student that unreleased material exists and that there was a leak worth hunting. Reworded to “Add search index pruning; track binarymodels26.R”.
The file comments. prune-search-index.sh’s header said it holds “decks, exercise answer keys, and side projects” out of the public repo; .gitignore’s comments spelled out the entire scheme, said the search index “leaks unreleased decks and answer keys,” and noted that answer keys stay out “regardless.” All trimmed to operational notes — the release recipe future-Dave needs, none of the rationale. Standing rule: tracked files carry operational notes only; the reasoning lives in this worklog, which is untracked. Verified every non-comment line of .gitignore byte-identical before and after, and that ex12026.qmd, ex12026answers.qmd, clarkreed.dta, and worklog.md are still ignored while ces.csv and binarymodels26.qmd are still published.
Rewrite mechanics, for next time: backup bundle at scratchpad/MLEfall26-pre-msg-rewrite.bundle (pre-rewrite main = d07c14c); refs/original/* deleted, reflog expired, git gc --prune=now; verified git diff origin/main HEAD~1 empty, i.e. only messages changed; pushed with --force-with-lease pinned to the old SHA. Post-push checks: 0 non-clavedark commits, 0 commits matching claude/anthropic, collaborators = clavedark only.
D14 — ces.csv is published in the repo; the exercise links it directly. Dave’s call, 2026-08-19, after being offered a gzipped version and a Brightspace-only fallback. The exercise said “Here’s a link to a dataset called ces.csv” and there was no link and no published file. Now !data/ces.csv in .gitignore, linked from exercise #1 and from the Data section of the Exercises & Code page, with data/README.md rewritten around two exceptions rather than one.
Amended 2026-08-19 (session 8b): the exercise links to the Data section, not to GitHub. The first version anchored the link on the ces.csv code span, pointing straight at the GitHub blob URL, and Dave read the sentence as having no link at all. It now reads [Here's a link](code.qmd#data) — plain words as the anchor, landing on the Data section of the Exercises & Code page, which is where the download link and the source credit already live. One place to maintain, and the GitHub-specific “click Download raw file” note stays on the code page instead of being repeated in the exercise. General lesson: don’t anchor a link on an inline code span when the sentence announces a link. Rationale: zero friction — students click one link, and the key’s read_csv(here::here("data", "ces.csv")) needs no change. Rejected the 1.0 MB gzip (13× smaller, and read_csv() reads .gz transparently — verified, 61,000 × 20) because Safari auto-gunzips .gz downloads, so some students would end up with a filename that doesn’t match the path in the code; that is a week-one support ticket for a saving nobody sees. Cost accepted: 13 MB, the largest tracked file in the repo, permanent in history (tracked payload 30 MB → 43 MB). The published page tells students GitHub won’t preview a file that size and to click Download raw file. Loose end: the source credit is the CES project site, not a formal citation — the ITT entry has a full one and this should match. Not written here because the exact Dataverse citation was not verified.
D11 — The key answers the question asked, quotes the question, and stops. Dave’s call, 2026-08-19, after two rounds of trimming. Three rules, all of which the key had been violating:

Every answer opens with its question, verbatim, as a blockquote. Students read the key days or weeks after doing the work, and a heading like “CDFs and PDFs” does not tell them what was asked. All ten questions plus the Part I and Part III preambles are quoted.
Answer the question and nothing adjacent. Question 1 asks what the PDFs and CDFs describe; the key had also explained why the CDF rather than the PDF is the link and how the three distributions differ in the tails. Both cut — the second is question 2’s job anyway. Question 6 says “describe the parts,” and the parts are the \(y=1\) term and the \(y=0\) term; that answer is now about those two and why the two-part form is written instead of the log-odds form, with the product-and-logs material demoted to one paragraph and the log-odds display gone.
No enrichment sections. The simulated-median panel, the two-panel comparison figure, and the delta-versus-simulation table were removed outright, not relabeled. A “Beyond the assignment” heading was the previous attempt and it was the wrong fix: length itself is the problem, because a key long enough to skim is a key nobody learns from afterwards. Same reasoning removed the se.fit-shortcut digression from question 10. Simulation-based intervals belong in a deck, not in an exercise key. Net: 957 → 882 lines with the question text added back in.

Also under this: the probit at-means chunk ended in a bare all.equal(...) that printed a stray TRUE into the prose. Now stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(...))) — silent on success, stops the render on failure, and a better habit to model.
D16 — The CES codebook is descriptions only, published complete. Dave’s call, 2026-08-24, in two steps. First: publish it, and tell students everything — “provide all the info they need… I’m interested in informing them completely.” That closed T7 against holding the item directions back to preserve the reverse-engineering work in question 8. Second, and the more consequential edit: no descriptive statistics. The first draft carried a frequency table for every categorical, summary statistics and a histogram for age, a missingness table, an empirical direction-evidence table, and a recode recipe. All of it went. “I really just want variable descriptions and nothing else — include only essential notes like which direction a variable runs.”
Rationale, and it is worth holding onto because it will come up again: a codebook answers what is this variable, and every distribution printed in it is a number the student should be generating themselves. Printing the frequencies doesn’t inform them, it does their count() calls for them — and it buries the one thing they can’t derive, which is what “Support” means on aca. The finished page is four tables of name/description/values/notes and about a page of prose. The supporting analysis that established the directions is not in it; it lives in this log and in the scratch profile, and the page says only that the directions were established from the data with aca as the worked example.
Corollary for future course documents: when a reference page and an exercise overlap, the reference gets the facts the student cannot compute, and nothing else.
D17 — Answer keys answer; they do not lecture (2026-08-24, Dave’s call). Dave read ex12026answers.qmd and cut it: “way too much prose and not in my voice.” The key had grown into a second lecture — roughly 320 words of exposition per question, with the Claude-slick constructions his style rules ban (aphoristic inversions: “A figure is an argument”; “Odds ratios are convenient because they are constant; they are treacherous for exactly the same reason”; “One coefficient, many marginal effects”; and reader-instructions like “Hold onto that sentence” and “worth memorizing”). Cut 38% of the answer prose and rewrote the rest plain and declarative. Rule going forward: the key answers what the question asked, once, and stops. Substance stays — every “comment on” and “discuss” prompt still gets a real answer, and the load-bearing points survive (the estimate beating the truth; the \(-693.147\) coin-flip benchmark; the odds-ratio-is-not-a-probability worked numbers; the .838-vs-.810 average-vs-at-means gap). What went is the second and third restatement of each. Precedent: the 2024 keys (ex12024answers.qmd) are nearly pure code with no prose at all; 2026 keeps prose because the discussion questions need answers, but the 2024 register is the direction of travel, not the lecture decks’. Code chunks were left byte-identical — verified.
D18 — Exercise #2 = write the Newton-Raphson maximizer (2026-08-25, Dave’s design). Replaces the D22 design entirely. Dave rejected both the old exercise and Claude’s family-swap proposal and set this: students write four functions — logit_ll, logit_score, logit_hessian, and fit_logit(X, y, tol, maxit) — then run the estimator on data they simulate and on the CES data, using the same model as Exercise #1 question 8 (vote ~ age + white + pro), not merely the same data. Rationale: the new skill for this cohort is not statistics, it is turning a formula they can find into a program with parts. So the math stays visible in llfmax26 (the update rule, the score, the Hessian, all in prose) and the code is hidden (D19) — finding the formula and writing the function is the assignment.
Design decisions inside it: - Signatures are given, bodies are not. The buildtemplate26 TODO device, plus a page on how functions work (arguments are inputs; anything the body uses that it did not create must be an argument, or R will silently reach into the workspace). No statistics given away. - A test per function, handed to them, so a stuck student learns which piece is broken: logit_ll at \(\beta = 0\) must equal \(n\ln(.5)\); logit_score checked against a central finite-difference gradient at an arbitrary \(\beta\) (at the solution a score that is wrong by a constant factor still passes); \(-H\) positive definite at \(\hat\beta\). - Agreement is asked two ways: against glm in decimal places, against the truth in standard errors. The second is new and fixes a real misread — an estimate 2.5 SEs off its truth is noise, and students read it as a broken estimator. - Three follow-ons, all three at Dave’s request so he can judge them: break your own gradient; build predicted probabilities from your own vcov; does the tolerance matter.
D19 — Hide the answer, temporarily and mechanically (2026-08-25). Two parts. (1) Three chunks in llfmax26.qmd set echo: false with a dated restore marker — dev2-step (the Newton step in code), nr (the whole loop plus the SEs), and fig-starts (which contains climb(), a second complete implementation). Deliberately left visible: the optim chunk (it is their independent check and the bridge to Ex #3), nr-history and the iteration-log figures (they show students the shape of the output they should produce without showing the code), and the one-parameter animation (scalar only). Dave’s instruction was to leave the code in the qmd and simply not reveal it, and not to worry about students having downloaded the earlier page or digging in the repo — the qmd itself is gitignored. (2) llfmax26.R, nr-logit.R, and compare-hand-glm.R added to .gitignore. Restore the three chunks after 2026-09-02; leave the gitignore entries permanently.
D20 — Exercises stand alone; comments describe code (2026-08-25, Dave’s rule). Two standing conventions, now in 2026/CLAUDE.md under Conventions. (1) No cross-references between exercises. An exercise or key never says “as in Exercise #1,” “you built this in Exercise #2,” or “next week Exercise #3 will…” — restate the model or the formula instead of pointing at another document. Dave allowed for exceptions but wants the default the other way. The Ex #2 rewrite is the argument for it: it broke every reference in Ex #3 at once (T11). (2) Code comments describe what the code does and nothing else — annotation to help a student write it, not narrative and not the lesson. Dave: “just describe what the code is doing — annotate to help students code.” The example he flagged was the ex #1 key’s llf chunk (“transcribed straight off the math… the two-part contribution… exactly what optim will want in Exercise #2”). Lessons belong in the prose around the chunk; forward references belong nowhere.
Applied this session to ex12026answers.qmd (3 cross-refs, 7 comment blocks), ex22026.qmd (4 cross-refs), and ex22026answers.qmd (3 cross-refs, 17 comment blocks). ex32026.qmd is riddled with them and was deliberately left alone — it is broken anyway and waiting on T11.
Note the tension with the deck voice. “Fuller exposition with deliberate redundancy” still governs lecture decks. Exercises, keys, and code comments are the other way: say it once, plainly. Both rules now sit in CLAUDE.md; do not let the deck rule leak into an exercise.
D21 — The Wk-3 build template runs on real ITT data, and gives nothing away (2026-08-30, Dave’s call). Dave: “It’s wordy… The template gives them a count, presents code including rpois and annotation naming the poisson, but then asks them how the data are distributed — not consistent or sensible. So make this an actual challenge.” Three changes.

Simulation-first is reversed. The old file opened with a rpois DGP whose comments named the distribution and the link, then asked students to diagnose \(y\). Now the file opens on real ITT country-years and the simulation moved to Step 8, where it does the job it is actually good at — checking that the estimator recovers a known truth, which glm agreement cannot establish. Nothing in the student file names the distribution, its parameter, or its link (verified against the rendered HTML: 0 occurrences of “Poisson”, “rpois”, “lambda”). The old file’s premise that the distribution is unseen is also dropped — likelihood26.qmd already gives the Poisson PMF, log-likelihood, link, and score. Dave: “they know the recipes b/c they have the slides.” The challenge is running the recipe, not discovering it.
y = scarring, and why. Checked all three ITT count outcomes as the y variable. All three fit and match glm; scarring wins on three grounds: it is already the running OLS example in predictionOLS26.qmd, where the prediction interval dips below zero and the text advertises count models, so the loop closes on the same outcome; at 9.7% zeros in the estimation sample it does not drag the discussion toward zero-inflation, which is not this file’s lesson (stealth is 29% zeros observed vs 8% predicted, a second failure mode that muddies the first); and its overdispersion is squarely the point Step 10 makes (Pearson dispersion 9.59). illtreatment is the fine second-best and correlates .86 with scarring.
A gradient step was added, and the polity quadratic dropped. optim with a numerical gradient lands ~0.002 from glm on the intercept, which fails an all.equal(tolerance = 1e-3) check — so the self-check would have printed FALSE for a correct build. Supplying the analytic score \(X'(y-\lambda)\) closes it to 6e-10, so the file now asks for negscore as its own TODO. That is the right fix rather than a loosened tolerance: they wrote the logit score for Exercise #2, and the transfer is the point. Separately, the deck’s p1 + p2 polity quadratic is not in this model: BFGS reports convergence == 0 and still lands 0.098 away from glm on it (collinear, badly scaled), which is a real lesson about believing convergence codes but the wrong one for a file whose whole device is “render, and all TRUE means you built it.”

D22 — The build template is a hand-rolled Newton-Raphson, mirroring Exercise #2 (2026-08-30, Dave’s call). optim is no longer the estimator; it is a check run at the end. The file is now 13 steps built on three functions and a loop, with Exercise #2’s signatures and argument order (beta, X, y), its fit_*(X, y, tol = 1e-8, maxit = 50) shape, and its return list (coef, se, vcov, loglik, iterations, converged, history). Names are neutral — mle_ll, mle_score, mle_hessian, fit_mle — because pois_ll would answer Step 1.
Three things that had to be worked out rather than assumed:

The \(\beta = \mathbf{0}\) test is cleaner here than in the logit. Ex #2 sets every coefficient to zero so \(\pi_i = 0.5\) and the weight is \(0.25\). Under the exp link the same move gives \(\lambda_i = 1\) for everybody, so \(\ell(\mathbf{0}) = -n - \sum\ln(y_i!)\), \(s(\mathbf{0}) = X'(y - \mathbf{1})\), and \(H(\mathbf{0}) = -X'X\) — no constant to carry at all. Each piece gets its own pass/fail row before the estimator runs.
Starting values matter more than they look. From \(\beta = \mathbf{0}\) NR takes 26 iterations on these data and the first step overshoots the intercept badly enough to drive the log-likelihood to \(-3.4\times10^{11}\) before it crawls back. From \(\beta_0 = (\ln\bar y, 0, \ldots)\) it takes 6, monotone throughout. The key uses the latter and says why; the student file tells them a better intercept guess exists without naming it.
The monotone-log-likelihood check needs a tolerance, and finding that out was worth it. The increments are \(325\), \(14.5\), \(0.052\), \(1.1\mathrm{e}{-6}\), \(-2.7\mathrm{e}{-12}\) — the last one negative, because at the top the log-likelihood stops changing at machine precision. A strict all(diff(loglik) > 0) printed FALSE on a fit that matches glm to ten decimals. Now > -1e-6, and the key explains the arithmetic rather than hiding it.

The intercept-only warm-up was dropped: with \(\ln\bar y\) starting values it converges in one iteration by construction, so it stopped being a test. The \(\beta = \mathbf{0}\) tests do that job better. optim moved to Step 10, where negating \(\ell\) and \(s\) is a minus sign rather than a new derivation, and where dropping gr shows the 0.0022 intercept gap that a numerical derivative costs.
D23 — How prediction26.qmd teaches uncertainty and the two approaches (2026-09-03, Dave’s request; design calls mine, all reversible). Dave: the Uncertainty section had no examples, the average-effects plot had no intervals, and the logic of at-means vs average vs simulated effects needed more elucidation, distinguishing the two simulation approaches and saying that KTW is the common one in the discipline. Choices made:

The average-effects plot gets a first-pass band, then the Uncertainty section replaces it. The band averages each case’s end-point-transformed interval (the 2024 loop’s move) and the prose says plainly that this is the uncertainty of a typical case, not of the average. “Average effects, two ways” then computes the delta and simulated bands and overlays the first-pass band as dotted lines. Verified: the rough band is wider (at Polity 0, width .0067 vs .0054 delta), as the quadratic-form argument says it must be. Mirrors the OLS companion deck, which flags its “median of the SEs” band the same way.
“Two simulation approaches” = simulate the parameters (KTW) vs resample the data (bootstrap). That is the split the 2024 deck made (“Simulating confidence intervals I / II”) and the one Dave’s “more commonly used” remark is about. KTW’s own expected-value vs predicted-value distinction (which the OLS deck develops) is kept as a paragraph inside the simulation section, with the binary-model point that the predicted value is a Bernoulli draw so the “prediction interval” is {0, 1}. The intro’s three-method list was reworded to match (its old third bullet, “simulation of the QI,” was ambiguous between the two readings).
At-means vs average, shown rather than asserted. Overlay of the two curves at border = 0: the at-means curve sits above the average everywhere. Not Jensen — composition: at-means holds ally at its mode (0) and 35% of the sample is allied (coef -0.84). Prose says so and names the nonlinearity as the second, smaller reason. A three-panel density of the 20,990 case-level predictions at Polity -10/0/10 shows what the average averages over.
Delta vs EPT needs a small sample to be visible. On the full data the two intervals agree to the third decimal everywhere, including extreme scenarios (checked lncaprat up to its max with ally = 1, deml = 10: delta lb .00086 vs EPT .00095). So the deck refits on a seeded random 500 dyad-years (26 disputes); there the delta lower bound crosses zero from Polity ≈ -4 on. Sweep showed n = 300, 500 spill clearly, n = 1000 barely (-0.0007), n = 2000 not at all.
Linear-combination SE gets a real model: dispute ~ ... + deml + I(deml^2). The square is significant (-0.0088, z = -5.8); the link-scale marginal effect crosses zero at Polity -4.5. SE built both from the written-out formula and as sqrt(diag(G V G')), shown equal.
KTW spaghetti figure (50 of the 1000 draws as curves, with the median and percentile curves of all 1000) as the picture of “each draw is a whole curve.” Bootstrap vs KTW densities at one profile, plus a four-technique table (EPT / delta / KTW / bootstrap) at that profile — all four agree to the third decimal (.0215-.0217 to .0278-.0281).
Added a “process, up front” callout (mirrors the OLS deck), a Take-away, and a References div.
The approach-by-technique table is gone (Dave, same day). “Really not clear”; the OLS deck had already cut it and replaced it with the two-sentence prose version (approach = which counterfactual, technique = how we bound it) plus a sentence saying what gets worked by hand and that average effects gets paired with both techniques at the end. Same here now. The pre-existing fig-max-me duplicate-label warning (chunk header + #| label) is untouched.

title: MLEfall26 — worklog
text:
T13 — Dave’s voice pass on the new prediction26.qmd sections (opened 2026-09-03). Resolved 2026-09-05: Dave edited through ~line 120, the rest swept; deck staged for release. The sections with no 2024 baseline: “The process, up front,” the symbols paragraphs under each approach, “At-means and average effects, side by side,” the KTW “why does this work” paragraphs and the spaghetti figure, the delta-vs-EPT pair (full data, then n = 500), the quadratic-model example, the bootstrap-vs-KTW comparison and four-way table, the Take-away. Also unreleased: no .gitignore un-ignore line exists for it yet, and code.qmd/index.qmd do not link it.
T9 — Releasing exercise #2. Built, rendered, verified; not released. Publishing here is opt-in by design, so nothing is public until Dave adds the un-ignore line and pushes. To release, follow the documented workflow: add !docs/ex22026.html to .gitignore (source stays ignored, exactly as ex12026.qmd does under D13 — the answers file and its HTML stay ignored permanently), quarto render ex22026.qmd, ./prune-search-index.sh, link it from wherever exercises are linked, re-render, re-prune, commit, push.
T12 — Reconsider the starting values in the binary materials (opened 2026-08-31; do not touch before 2026-09-02). Dave: “why don’t we do this in the binomial models, ie start with mean y plus k-1 zeros for starting values instead of all zeros?” Tested rather than argued. On the course dispute logit (dispute ~ lncaprat + border + deml, n = 20,990) Newton-Raphson takes 8 iterations from \(\mathbf{0}\) and 6 from \((\mathrm{logit}(\bar y), 0, \ldots)\) — same estimates, monotone either way. So it helps, but it is not a repair.
The mechanism, which is the part worth teaching. It is not distance: \(\beta = \mathbf{0}\) is further from the intercept-only solution in link space for the logit (\(|\mathrm{logit}(.045)| =
3.05\)) than for the Poisson (\(|\ln 8.13| = 2.10\)). It is the weight Newton divides by. Logit weight at \(\mathbf{0}\) is \(\pi(1-\pi) = 0.25\) against \(0.042\) at the solution — 6x too steep, so the step comes out too short; and \(0.25\) is the maximum \(\pi(1-\pi)\) can take, so \(\beta = \mathbf{0}\) is the most conservative start a logit has. Poisson weight at \(\mathbf{0}\) is \(\lambda = 1\) against \(8.13\) — 8x too flat, so the step overshoots.
Verified the falsifiable implication rather than stopping at the story: simulated Poissons sweeping \(\bar y\) = 0.25, 0.64, 1.15, 1.88, 5.2, 9.2, 23.2 take 7, 6, 6, 7, 13, 23, 58 iterations from \(\mathbf{0}\) and 5 from \(\ln\bar y\) every time. Below \(\bar y \approx 1\) zeros are fine; above it the cost grows without bound (first-iteration log-likelihood \(-1.9\times10^{26}\) at \(\bar y = 23\)). The bounded inverse link is what protects the logit.
Nothing was changed. Exercise #2 is live and due 2026-09-02, and it already asks students to pick starting values and justify them — so a student who does this is rewarded, not contradicted. After that date, consider it for llfmax26 and nr-logit.R as pedagogy: it gives “say why you picked them” an actual answer. One sentence of it went into buildtemplate26answers.qmd Step 7 now, stated as a fact about binary models rather than a pointer to another document (D20).
T10 — Restore the llfmax26 chunks after 2026-09-02. Resolved 2026-09-05: all three chunks back to echo: true, header note removed, re-rendered, pruned, staged with the ex #2 key. grep "HIDDEN FOR EXERCISE #2" llfmax26.qmd, set all three back to echo: true, re-render, re-prune. There is a note at the top of the qmd. If this is missed, the best deck in the course stays permanently missing its Newton-Raphson code.
T11 — Exercise #3 now contradicts Exercise #2. ex32026.qmd opens “There you built a binomial estimator with the link as an argument” and its Part I asks students to swap the link on that estimator. Neither is true any more — Ex #2 builds a Newton-Raphson logit with no link argument and no optim. Part II (real dispute data, the five-decimal glm comparison, the run-down-the- discrepancy question) is still good and is arguably better now: their exact-Hessian NR matches glm to nine decimals, so handing the same problem to optim and losing decimals is a sharp contrast. Not touched this session — Dave has not asked.
T8 — Exercise #2 redesign. Diagnosed and designed 2026-08-24 (session 11); nothing built. Design memo: 2026/ex2-redesign-memo.md. Proposal in one line: stop swapping the link (a one-line edit of a log-likelihood they were handed) and swap the family, run through a fixed seven-step protocol they reuse all term — look at \(y\), write the likelihood, choose a link that respects the parameter’s support, code the negative LLF, warm up intercept-only against a hand derivation, verify (recover a simulated truth + numerical gradient + the canned routine), interpret one quantity of interest. Recommended family: the exponential duration model, \(\ell = \sum [x_i\beta -
\exp(x_i\beta)y_i]\) — two terms, absent from every lecture file, the log link is load-bearing rather than decorative, an analytic intercept-only check (\(\hat\beta_0 = -\log\bar y\)), and it on-ramps Week 11. Verified in scratchpad/expcheck.R: recovery exact at large \(n\), gradient ~1e-4, analytic check matches to six decimals, and survreg/glm(Gamma(log)) return \(-\hat\beta\) with SEs matching to five decimals — a real “do they match?” moment about parameterization. Two forks are Dave’s: (a) one family for everyone vs. one per student (recommend: one family, per-student seeds); (b) whether Ex #2 stays purely simulated (recommend: yes; real data stays in Ex #3). Also flagged: the AI paragraph in ex22026.qmd claims “a bot cannot fake recovering a truth you set,” which is not true of the assignment as written; and “do they agree?” should be scaled — \((\hat\beta - \beta)/\widehat{SE}\) — since at \(n = 2{,}000\) an estimate 2.5 SEs off its truth is noise that students will read as a broken estimator.
T5 — Cloglog/Exercise-#2 collision. Resolved 2026-08-19 (session 5): Ex#1 Part II reverted to the logit, see D9. Exercise #2 was never edited and needs no change.
T6 — Releasing exercise #1. Resolved 2026-08-19 (session 7) — built and staged, see D12. Awaiting Dave’s commit and push only.
T7 — Whether to publish the CES codebook, and what it costs question 8. Resolved 2026-08-24 (session 10) — publish it complete, see D16. The option of holding the direction information back so the traps stay traps was on the table and Dave rejected it: “I’m interested in informing them completely.” Staged; awaiting his commit and push only.

Done. Built and released cescodebook26.qmd. It went through two versions and the second one is the one that matters — see D16. The first draft was a full statistical codebook (frequency tables computed at render time, age summary and histogram, missingness table, direction-evidence table, recode recipe). Dave cut all of it: descriptions only, plus the notes a student cannot derive from the file. What shipped is four tables — identifiers/demographics, politics, policy items, each row name / description / values / notes — a two-paragraph header (no survey weights; the labels give the side, not the question), and a short note saying the item directions were established from the data with aca as the worked example. No R chunks at all; the page is static markdown, which also means it can’t drift when the extract changes and can’t be checked automatically either.
Then the release, following the four-step workflow above: .gitignore un-ignores cescodebook26.qmd and docs/cescodebook26.html; code.qmd’s CES entry links it; ex12026.qmd’s “Variable descriptions are in the data” — false, the CSV has column names and nothing else — now reads that the file carries no descriptions, links the codebook, and warns that several policy items don’t run the direction their names suggest. All three pages re-rendered, index re-pruned. Not committed, not pushed — that’s Dave’s.
The substantive finding. Seven of the twenty variables are policy items whose labels give the side but not the question, and two of them run backwards from what the variable name suggests: aca == "Support" means support repealing the ACA (Dave’s own 2024 key had this right — repealaca <- ifelse(aca == "Support", 1, 0)), and mandmin == "Support" means support eliminating mandatory minimums. Both are silent errors: the recode runs, glm converges, the sign is just wrong. Also non-obvious: hispanic is a follow-up with a skip pattern (5,180 of the 5,800 race-Hispanic respondents are NA on it, so NA ≠ “not Hispanic”); know_governor is the party the respondent named, not whether they were right; and educ sorts to nonsense alphabetically.
Verified. Direction of every policy item established empirically rather than from remembered question wording — cross-tabulated each against pid7 and votechoice. aca == "Support": 83.3% of Trump voters, 9.5% of Biden voters. wall == "Support": 88.7% / 8.6%. cleanair == "Support": 23.5% / 90.2%. mandmin == "Support": 53.7% / 86.1% — the least polarized item in the file, and the one whose direction the name alone will not give you. know_governor confirmed as an answer rather than a correctness flag by checking states where the true party is unambiguous: 83.4% of Californians say Democrat, 83.7% of Floridians say Republican, and 78.5% of Massachusetts respondents say Republican for a Republican governor in a very blue state. N = 61,000, matching the 2020 CES common content; 232 exact duplicate rows once the index column is dropped, which is what chance produces with 19 coarse categoricals and 61,000 rows — not a merge artifact.
Release verified too. git check-ignore -v shows leading ! on both new paths (.gitignore:53:!cescodebook26.qmd, .gitignore:71:!docs/cescodebook26.html). The pruner reports 60/60 entries across 10 published pages with nothing held out, and a per-page count of the index confirms only published pages are in it — ex12026answers, llfmax26, and the unreleased decks are all absent. Both new links resolve in docs/ex12026.html and docs/code.html. The rendered codebook’s tables parse correctly — checked every row for four cells, because race == "Hispanic" | hispanic == "Yes" puts a literal pipe inside a pandoc pipe-table cell (it survives because it sits inside a code span, but it is exactly the kind of thing that silently eats a column).
One thing the pruner caught, worth repeating. Rendering a single file updates docs/search.json in place, so rendering the codebook while it was still unpublished put ten of its entries into the tracked index — the August leak’s exact mechanism, on a page that at that moment was held out. ./prune-search-index.sh removed them. Then, after publishing, the index had to be rebuilt again, because the intervening single-file renders of ex12026/code didn’t re-add the codebook’s entries and it would have shipped unsearchable. The note, answered. Rewrote it around the two-step lookup: R looks inside the function first (arguments, plus anything the body made), then in your workspace. So the fix is simply to make it an argument — the local binding always wins, and the leak only happens for names you forgot to declare. Then the part that was missing, how to prove there is no leak: rename the outside objects so the names disagree (design/outcome, rm(X, y)) and call the function again. Dave’s note. “Why does 6 indicate there’s a bug, but 2 doesn’t? Would 4? What’s the threshold here? Why?” A fair hit: the passage asserted 2-versus-6 without justifying the cut.
Computed it rather than hand-waving. The relevant probability is not \(P(\lvert z\rvert > c)\) for one coefficient but \(P(\text{any of } k > c) = 1-(1-p)^k\), because you look at all \(k\) and react to the largest. With \(k = 3\): over 2 in about one run in 8; over 3, one in 124; over 4, one in 5,300; over 6, one in 170 million. That table is now in the exercise, and it makes “would 4?” answerable — yes, distinctly.
The note also exposed a real sloppiness. I had folded two different thresholds into one number. They are separate questions and the text now separates them: at 3, go look — not because it is proof but because the decision is lopsided (checking working code costs ten minutes; not checking broken code costs a reported result) — and at 6, stop calling it luck.
And the answer that beats a threshold, which is available here precisely because the truth was chosen rather than estimated: change the seed and refit. Sampling noise moves; a bug sits still. Verified with eight seeds on the correct estimator — max \(\lvert z\rvert\) ran 0.77 to 1.72 and never reached 2, so a \(z\) that stays at 6 across re-runs is diagnostic. The key flags this as the answer worth rewarding, since a student who proposes it has understood that the ratio is a claim about repeated samples.

Addendum 5 — the Hessian’s lambda * X line needed a dimension walk. Dave: “this looks like a kxn matrix times (lxn *nxk) … how do the dimensions sort out here?” The reading that trips people is treating * as matrix multiplication. It is elementwise, and it changes no shape: lambda has length \(n\) — exactly one column of an \(n \times k\) matrix stored column-major — so it restarts at the top of each column and element \((i,j)\) comes out \(\lambda_i x_{ij}\). Row \(i\) is scaled by \(\lambda_i\), the result is still \(n \times k\), and t(X) %*% it is \((k \times n)(n \times k) = k
\times k\). Verified against diag(lambda) %*% X and against an explicit \(\sum_i \lambda_i x_i'x_i\) loop on a 3-by-2 toy; all three agree.
The comment in the key now says * is elementwise and not matrix multiplication, and the prose after the chunk carries the walk, the reason (\(X'(\Lambda X)\) by associativity, so \(\Lambda\) is never built — 6.4 MB saved at \(n = 913\), 80 GB at \(n = 100{,}000\)), and the hazard: recycling is silent, so a wrong-length vector scales the wrong cells with no error and a result of exactly the right shape. Confirmed the \(\beta = \mathbf{0}\) test catches it, since \(H(\mathbf{0}) = -X'X\) is unforgiving about the weights.
